Ramya, R. et al: Battery Management System …… Archives for Technical Sciences 2025, 33(2), 430-441
 Electric vehicles (EVs) are seeing tremendous market expansion due to their efficiency and zero
 emissions. However, a battery's lifespan, cost, performance, and safety could all be impacted by other
 factors. Thus, battery management is required to improve a battery's performance under a range of
 operating conditions. One device that can regulate the behaviour of heated batteries is the battery thermal
 management system. Phase change material cooling systems, liquid cooling systems, air-cooling
 systems, and direct refrigerant cooling systems are among the BTMS technologies discussed in this
 article. We analyse the weights, sizes, prices, and capabilities of various systems [19].

 Since Li-ion batteries outperform other types, they are the most often utilized kind in electric vehicles
 (EVs). The BMS, which is the core component of an electric car, may improve a battery's lifespan,
 safety, performance, and operation. One of the most crucial aspects of installing a BMS is assessing the
 condition of the Li-ion batteries, as it is necessary for the stable and secure functioning of batteries.
 Recently, researchers have concentrated on creating digital twin models utilizing ML approaches and
 cloud computing to automate and enhance the BMS state estimate process. [20].

 Because of the enormous volume of battery data generated over its operating life, cloud computing has
 been embraced by the scientific community for data storage and analysis. This cloud-based digital
 solution offers a more flexible and effective option than more conventional approaches that could need
 significant hardware investments. Machine learning is rapidly becoming a key technique for gleaning
 insights and patterns from massive amounts of observational data. A cloud-based, AI-enhanced BMS is
 therefore expected to be created in the future [21].

 BTMS employ PCM to regulate the battery's temperature and enhance performance with the help of an
 ANN. Investigating methods for comparing various battery heat management system types also seems
 beneficial given the rising use of AI in numerous industries. [22]. The BMS solutions, which call for a
 mix of hardware and software, include battery status estimates, fault detection, monitoring, and control
 responsibilities. This research extensively analyses the most recent machine-learning techniques for
 BMS. It distinguishes various methods according to their principles, types, structures, and ways of
 evaluating performance [23].

 Businesses may construct and test whole buildings and complete assembly processes by constructing
 digital twins of their goods and manufacturing processes. This accelerates the transition to high-volume
 production while maintaining the quality of the end product. The hardest aspect of driving an electric
 vehicle is managing the battery. [24] investigates the types, architectures, underlying theories, and
 performance evaluations of the most modern machine learning approaches for battery management
 systems in high-power applications, such smart grids and electric vehicles [25].

 Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are employed in battery temperature predictive control models
 to forecast temperature changes over a specified prediction horizon. Adding forecast and historical data
 to the model greatly improves its accuracy and applicability. For median temperature estimations, the
 best model outperformed the others, with a mean absolute error of 0.27 °C.

  This model's ability to deliver accurate predictions across various contexts highlights its potential for
 broader applications in energy management, offering significant improvements in battery temperature
 regulation and overall system efficiency [26].

 Battery Electric Vehicles (BEVs) that use hybrid battery technology combine high-power and high-
 energy battery packs to maximize performance. A cloud-based energy management method that makes
 use of the Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient algorithm is advised in order to improve safety, lower
 energy loss, and save aging costs. This method reduces training epochs by 20.0% and 98.5% compared
 to typical Deep Q-Learning methods, and it also greatly minimizes energy waste and aging expenses
 [27].

 PROPOSED METHODOLOGY

 Key battery metrics including voltage, current, and temperature are monitored by the suggested battery
 management system using artificial intelligence and the Internet of Things. These parameters are
 measured using sensors and are updated in real-time by an ESP32 and Raspberry Pi controller. The
 system utilizes the Thing Speak cloud platform to aggregate and analyse the data, and it employs a
 Support Vector Machine learning algorithm to enhance predictive accuracy and decision-making, which
 is shown in Figure 1.

 Internet of Things-based battery pack monitoring is used to track and manage the battery pack specified
 in the suggested battery management system. IOT technology tracks battery health via sensors,
 controllers, and online apps. Sensors that detect temperature, voltage, and current are used to get these
 readings. The voltage and current sensors continually check the battery's voltage and current,
 respectively. The voltage and current sensors can detect currents up to 5A and voltages up to 25V DC.
 To assess the battery's performance, the temperature sensor will keep an eye on its temperature. After
 processing the sensor data, the controller shows the results on the LCD.The ESP 32 controller collects

 For batteries and thermal management systems, among other hardware and software components, to
 work well, they must cooperate and be controlled. Among the parts of the BMS are a position machine,
 temperature monitors, a cut-off field-effect transistor, a cell voltage monitor, a cell voltage balance, and
 a real-time clock. There are several chips available nowadays that have PMS built in. The capabilities
 of freestanding, fully integrated systems can be matched by simple Analog front ends with
 microprocessors for monitoring and balancing. In various systems, functional components are placed
 differently. Compared to existing protection circuit designs, the proposed BMS includes more sensors,
 allowing for enhancements like precise alarms and controls to avoid overcharging, over discharge, and
 overheating. Battery factors such as cell temperature, current, and voltage must be monitored and
 evaluated using a sensor network. The battery parameters are monitored and stored in a Raspberry Pi
 controller, a minicomputer used for real-time implementation and to fetch Python software. The high-

KEY RESULTS / BREAK-EVEN THRESHOLDS
IMPLICATION
1. Depot charging
Daily energy: 25.68 kWh; 7.4 kW AC charging takes ~3.86 h. Charger cost: ₹50,000 hardware + ₹30,000 installation + ₹10,000 DISCOM connection, increased to ₹99,000/vehicle for N+1 redundancy. Software and AMC: ₹15,000/year.
Depot off-peak tariffs: ₹5.50–9/kWh; public DC retail: ₹18–24/kWh. At ₹4.50/kWh, EV energy costs ₹0.64/km; at ₹8.50, ₹1.21/km; at ₹12, ₹1.71/km.
Depot charging is essential. The report's ₹12/kWh sensitivity turns negative, and public DC retail tariffs are typically higher. Charger infrastructure must be included in TCO.
2. Vehicle uptime
Baseline downtime: 3.5 h/month—0.5 h queues/port unavailability, 1 h planned maintenance, 1.5 h repairs and 0.5 h charger failure. Net cost of lost operating time: ₹200.46/hour.
Baseline loss: ₹702/month, ₹0.135/km or ₹42,097 over five years. Break-even: 25.4 total downtime hours/month, leaving 21.9 additional hours beyond baseline. A reported ~75 h/month without depot charging produces a −28.4% result.
Reliable depot access is a contractual operating requirement, not an automatic property of the vehicle. Charging queues and repairs can erase savings.
3. Battery replacement risk
Main eight-year case assumes no pack replacement. The report's replacement sensitivity uses an earlier nominal, vehicle-only comparison basis.
No replacement: ₹5.75/km, +14.5% EV advantage. ₹4 lakh replacement: ₹7.04/km, −4.5%; ₹8 lakh: ₹8.32/km, −23.5%; ₹12 lakh: ₹9.60/km, −42.6%.
Even a ₹4 lakh replacement reverses the earlier comparison. Battery warranty, capacity-retention guarantees and replacement terms are critical. Recalculate scenarios on the final NPV-inclusive basis before comparing them with the headline result.
4. Battery life and EFC
Battery-side throughput: 8,012 kWh/year. EFC estimates: 178/year using nominal 45 kWh capacity; 181.3 using usable 44.2 kWh; 197.8 using wall energy divided by nominal capacity.
Consistent calculation gives 178 EFC/year and 16.85 years to 3,000 cycles, versus 197.8 EFC/year and 15.16 years on the published basis. Calendar-ageing estimates range from 3.7 years to 80% capacity under a measured linear model to 13.3 years under a √t model at 40°C.
The published EFC figure overstates cycle throughput by 11.1% because it mixes wall energy with battery capacity. Cycle life does not guarantee service life; calendar ageing may dominate.

Three-Level Threshold — Normal: 32–35 psi, 30–50°C. Warning: below 28 psi or above 60°C. Critical: below 22 psi or above 70°C — VCU alert triggered at each level.
Leak Detection — Rate of pressure drop monitored continuously. Rapid or gradual loss flagged before reaching critical threshold, logged to VCU and cloud.
System Value — Correct pressure reduces rolling resistance and extends range. Early detection prevents mid-shift tyre failures on revenue-earning vehicles.

DELIVERABLE ANALYSIS · AI & CONNECTED MOBILITY ECOSYSTEM

Requirements Framework & Gap Analysis
for the 2035 EV Platform Proposal

Defines what each digital-layer pillar must specify, maps data flows and AI functions, then audits the existing proposal and Suzuki Connect against these requirements.

5 Pillars Analyzed Ola Electric Case · UN R156 · ISO 24089 Status: Gap Analysis
Framing note: The Ola Electric 2021–22 failure is the baseline for every requirement below — 80,000 complaints/month, sensor faults invisible until breakdown, big-bang software pushes with no rollback, and a rider-facing "black box." A credible proposal must either solve each of those failure modes explicitly, or acknowledge the gap. Generic features without data flows and decision logic are insufficient for a proposal at this level.
PART 1

Requirements Framework — What Each Pillar Must Specify

SYSTEM DATA FLOW ARCHITECTURE — 5-LAYER REFERENCE
VEHICLE
Sensors & CAN-bus
BMS · IMU · GPS · Motor current · Fault codes
→
On-board ECU / TCU
Edge pre-processing · OTA slot B
→
Edge Gateway
4G/LTE compression · local anomaly flag
→
Cloud Ingest
Time-series DB · event stream
→
AI / Analytics
CNN/LSTM · Risk scorer · Digital twin
→
Apps & Dashboards
Fleet ops · Driver · Rider
PILLAR 1

Telematics & Vehicle Data

Sub-domain Data Collected (must specify) Flow Path AI Function Decision / Action Enabled
Battery / Power
  • Cell-level voltage & temperature (not pack-average)
  • State-of-Health (SoH) — degradation curve, not binary
  • Charge/discharge C-rate per cycle
  • CNG fuel-pressure & injector status (variant-specific)
 BMS → TCU
TCU → Cloud @ 1Hz
Cloud → Battery ML model 		SoH degradation regression; thermal runaway early-warning classifier; capacity-fade forecast Flag cell imbalance before pack failure; schedule battery swap/service proactively; adjust charging limits per vehicle age
Motion & Powertrain
  • IMU: 3-axis accelerometer + gyroscope at ≥50 Hz
  • Wheel-speed per axle
  • Motor current draw (phase-level)
  • Controller temperature, torque demand vs output
 CAN-bus → ECU
ECU edge-filter → Cloud
Cloud → CNN/LSTM 		Vibration-pattern fault classification (motor bearing wear, inverter fault); road-condition inference from IMU 97%+ motor/inverter fault classification; route-difficulty scoring for duty-cycle calibration
Positioning & Connectivity
  • GPS lock-time and positional accuracy (HDOP)
  • Antenna hardware revision (critical: Ola's GPS mismatch was invisible without this)
  • Connectivity uptime, packet-loss rate per vehicle
 GPS module → TCU
TCU → Cloud metadata 		Hardware-revision mismatch detector; connectivity-stability score feeds OTA risk model Block OTA push to vehicles with unstable connectivity; detect GPS antenna/firmware mismatch before rider impact
Software & Firmware State
  • Firmware version per ECU/module
  • Hardware revision per component
  • Active fault codes (DTC) + historical fault log
  • OTA slot status (A/B), last update timestamp
 ECU → Cloud manifest
Cloud → Risk scorer 		Version/revision matrix compatibility check; fault-history weighting in risk scoring Prevent mismatched firmware reaching riders; auto-rollback to slot A on post-update fault spike
Usage Patterns
  • km/day, trips/day, idle time
  • Charging windows & session duration
  • Duty cycle intensity (urban stop-go vs highway)
 ECU → aggregated daily
Cloud → Digital twin 		Per-vehicle duty-cycle model for fine-tuning failure prediction; charging behavior anomaly detection Customize maintenance intervals per actual usage; detect vehicle misuse or overloading
PILLAR 2

Fleet & Battery Management

Sub-domain What Must Be Specified Flow Path AI Function Decision / Action Enabled
OTA Software Rollout
  • Risk-scoring model features: hardware revision, sensor calibration age, fault history, connectivity stability
  • Cohort size and expansion gate criteria (not just "staged")
  • A/B partition (slot A / slot B) architecture per vehicle
  • Rollback trigger definition (fault-rate threshold post-update)
  • Compliance: UN R156 SUMS + ISO 24089 audit trail
 Cloud → Risk scorer
Risk score → Cohort assign
OTA push → Slot B
Validation pass → Activate 		Risk-score ranking; post-deployment fault-rate monitoring; anomaly triggers rollback signal Zero-downtime update cycle; automatic fleet-wide rollback if fault rate exceeds threshold; audit-ready SUMS log
Fleet Operator Dashboard
  • Multi-vehicle view (500+ vehicles) — not single-vehicle
  • OTA deployment status per vehicle/cohort
  • Active fault summary with severity triage
  • Predicted downtime calendar (when, which vehicles)
  • Battery SoH fleet-wide distribution
 Cloud DB → Fleet API
Fleet API → Operator UI 		Fleet-level anomaly ranking; maintenance workload forecasting; route availability prediction Prioritise workshop slots before predicted failures; pull high-risk vehicles before they strand riders
Battery Lifecycle Management
  • Per-cell SoH trajectory over vehicle lifetime
  • Cycle count vs rated cycle life
  • Thermal event history
  • Second-life eligibility threshold (SoH %)
 BMS → Cloud time-series
Cloud → Degradation model 		Remaining useful life (RUL) regression; second-life readiness classifier Schedule battery replacement at 70–80% SoH before range anxiety impacts riders; flag second-life candidates for stationary storage
PILLAR 3

Driver & Rider Apps

Sub-domain What Must Be Specified Flow Path AI Function Decision / Action Enabled
Driver Interface — Fault UX
  • Plain-language fault triage: exactly three states — "Safe to continue," "Reboot required," "Book service now"
  • No raw DTC codes on primary display
  • Screen-frozen fallback behaviour (audio/haptic)
  • Driver-visible OTA notification before update applies
 ECU fault → Cloud NLP
NLP → Dash message
Message → Driver CTA 		DTC-to-plain-language translation model; severity classification (safe/caution/stop) Driver acts within their competence; eliminates "frozen display — no indicator visible" Ola failure mode
Rider-Facing Data Transparency
  • Explicit disclosure: what data is collected, who sees it, retention period
  • No remote vehicle disable without driver confirmation
  • No silent income-pattern or GPS sale to third parties
  • Driver dashboard showing their own data footprint
 Data policy → In-app
Consent log → Cloud 		None required — policy and UI design decision, not algorithmic Removes #1 e-rickshaw/EV trust barrier; regulatory data-minimisation compliance (DPDP Act 2023)
Proactive Driver Notifications
  • Predicted maintenance alert (vehicle-specific, timed to off-shift)
  • Charging window recommendation (grid load + SoH-aware)
  • OTA update schedule — when and expected duration
 AI prediction → Cloud
Cloud → Driver app push 		Failure prediction output triggers notification; charging optimisation model Driver schedules service voluntarily during downtime, not mid-shift; charging cost optimisation
PILLAR 4

Safety & Predictive Maintenance

Sub-domain What Must Be Specified Flow Path AI Function Decision / Action Enabled
Fault Classification — Motor & Inverter
  • Input signals: vibration (IMU), phase current, temperature
  • Model architecture: CNN/LSTM hybrid (not rule-based threshold)
  • Accuracy benchmark: ≥97% classification (cited in proposal)
  • Fault class taxonomy: bearing wear, winding insulation, IGBT fault, overcurrent
 IMU+current → Edge buffer
Edge → Cloud CNN/LSTM
Output → Fleet alert 		CNN extracts vibration frequency features; LSTM models temporal degradation progression; ensemble reduces false-positive rate Fault type identified before driver notices symptom; maintenance crew dispatched with correct part, not generic inspection
Failure Timeline Prediction
  • Prediction horizon: days-to-failure (not binary fault/no-fault)
  • Baseline accuracy: ±25 days before per-vehicle fine-tuning; ±12 days after (cited)
  • Fine-tuning trigger: per-vehicle usage pattern deviation
  • 100% detection rate for wear-driven failures — quantified from field validation
 Usage history → Cloud model
Per-vehicle fine-tune
Output → Maintenance calendar 		RUL regression with per-vehicle fine-tuning; multi-country heterogeneous fleet validation (India included) Failure flagged ~12 days in advance; service scheduled during off-shift; zero unplanned mid-route breakdown
Digital Twin Validation
  • Twin scope: motor current, thermal behaviour, vibration profile per vehicle model
  • Used as pre-deployment check for every OTA update
  • Triggered by: sensor anomaly flag, hardware revision change, new firmware version
 Sensor telemetry → Twin
OTA package → Twin test
Pass/fail → Rollout gate 		Physics-informed simulation; anomaly deviation detection against expected twin response GPS antenna/firmware mismatch caught in twin before reaching riders; no reactive vehicle-by-vehicle fixes
PILLAR 5

AI / Data Layer Connecting Everything

Component What Must Be Specified Inputs Outputs Connects Which Pillars
Risk-Scoring Engine Feature vector: hardware revision, sensor calibration age, fault history count, connectivity uptime %. Scoring frequency, cohort-size logic, expansion gate thresholds Telemetry + metadata Vehicle risk rank (0–100); cohort assignment; rollout hold flag Telematics → Fleet Management → OTA
CNN/LSTM Fault Classifier Input signal sampling rate; model update cadence; threshold for escalating from "monitor" to "alert" to "ground vehicle" IMU · current · temp Fault class + confidence score; days-to-failure estimate Telematics → Safety → Driver App → Fleet Dashboard
Digital Twin Engine Vehicle model variants covered; deviation tolerance before alert; twin update frequency as real-world data accumulates Sensor stream + OTA package Pass/fail for OTA; deviation anomaly score; validated maintenance schedule Telematics → Safety → Fleet Management → OTA
DTC-to-Language NLP Fault code taxonomy covered; language/dialect support (Hindi, regional); fallback if connectivity lost CAN fault codes Three-state driver instruction; service-booking deep link Telematics → Driver App
Data Governance Layer Retention period per data class; anonymisation before third-party use; driver consent management; DPDP Act 2023 compliance log All telemetry streams Consent-gated data release; audit trail; anonymised research export All pillars → Regulatory & rider trust
PART 2

Gap Analysis — Proposal vs. Suzuki Connect vs. Requirements

ADDRESSED Requirement is substantively covered with specifics
PARTIAL Mentioned but lacks technical depth or data-flow detail
GAP Not addressed — must be added before proposal is credible
Requirement Pillar Proposal Doc Suzuki Connect Gap / What Must Be Added
Cell-level battery telemetry (voltage, temp, SoH per cell) Telematics ADDRESSED GAP Suzuki Connect reports pack-level status only. Proposal correctly specifies cell-level. Needs to add: sampling rate, time-series retention period, and protocol (BMS → CAN → TCU).
CNN/LSTM fault classification (motor, inverter) Safety / AI ADDRESSED GAP Well cited (≥97% accuracy, vibration/current/temp inputs). Missing: fault class taxonomy, false-positive rate target, on-edge vs. cloud inference split, model update cadence.
A/B partition OTA rollback (slot A / slot B) Fleet Mgmt ADDRESSED GAP Proposal correctly cites this as the fix for "scooter won't turn on after update." Needs: rollback trigger definition (which fault-rate threshold activates it) and who authorises manual rollback for fleet ops.
Failure prediction timeline (days-to-failure, field-validated) Safety ADDRESSED GAP Quantified well (±25d → ±12d post fine-tuning; 100% wear-failure detection). Missing: what happens when prediction confidence is low — escalation path and human review workflow.
No remote kill-switch / transparent data use (rider trust) Rider App ADDRESSED GAP Correctly identifies BMS remote-disable as the #1 trust barrier. Needs to reference DPDP Act 2023 compliance specifically, and name what data is not collected (income patterns, route monetisation).
Risk-scored staged OTA rollout Fleet Mgmt ADDRESSED GAP Feature vector listed (HW revision, calibration age, fault history, connectivity). Missing: cohort expansion gate criteria — what metric/threshold unlocks the next cohort? Who approves expansion?
Digital twin pre-deployment validation Safety / AI ADDRESSED GAP Twin scope specified (motor current, thermal, vibration). Needs: which vehicle model variants have twins on day one, twin update latency as real data accumulates, and deviation tolerance threshold.
GPS hardware revision tracking (antenna/firmware mismatch detection) Telematics PARTIAL GAP The Ola GPS mismatch story is cited, but the mechanism to prevent it is not fully specified. Must add: hardware revision logged per component per vehicle in the fleet manifest, with automatic compatibility matrix check on every OTA push. The risk scorer must explicitly include GPS antenna HW revision as a feature.
Driver plain-language fault UX ("safe / reboot / service") Driver App PARTIAL GAP Three states named. Missing: (1) what happens when display itself is frozen — audio/haptic fallback; (2) whether translation happens on-edge (offline capable) or requires connectivity; (3) regional language support (Hindi minimum for Indian fleet).
Fleet operator dashboard (multi-vehicle, not single-owner) Fleet Mgmt PARTIAL GAP Explicitly flagged as absent from Suzuki Connect. Proposal acknowledges fleet-op context but does not describe the dashboard. Must add: key views (OTA deployment status, fault triage, predicted downtime calendar, battery SoH distribution), role-based access (fleet owner vs. mechanic vs. driver), alert routing.
UN R156 SUMS + ISO 24089 compliance Fleet Mgmt / AI PARTIAL GAP Both standards are cited correctly. Not yet specified: what the SUMS audit trail contains (update manifest, vehicle list, rollout timestamp, rollback events), who the nominated SUMS responsible person is, how the ISO 24089 engineering evidence package is generated from the platform.
Continuous telemetry pipeline architecture Telematics / AI PARTIAL GAP Data classes listed correctly. Missing infrastructure detail: streaming protocol (MQTT / AMQP), time-series database choice, data compression at edge (critical for rural connectivity), and what happens when vehicle is offline — local buffer duration and sync behaviour.
CNG variant sensor coverage Telematics PARTIAL GAP Mentioned as "fuel-system sensors for CNG variants" but not elaborated. Needs: which specific CNG sensors (pressure, temperature, injector duty cycle), whether the same CNN/LSTM models apply or CNG requires separate classifiers, and how the AI layer handles dual-fuel variants.
Battery second-life / RUL management Fleet Mgmt GAP GAP Not addressed anywhere in the proposal. For a 2035 vehicle, battery lifecycle economics are a major differentiator. Must add: SoH threshold for replacement vs. second-life routing, RUL regression model, integration with battery recycling/swap partners, and how this data is surfaced to fleet operators.
Data governance / DPDP Act 2023 compliance Rider App / AI GAP GAP Rider data trust is discussed but Indian regulatory compliance is not named. Must add: data retention periods per class, consent collection mechanism, right-to-erasure workflow, and what is excluded from third-party data sharing. Critical for commercial fleet operators operating under DPDP Act 2023.
Offline / degraded-connectivity fail-safes Telematics / Safety GAP GAP Indian rural and peri-urban routes have intermittent 4G. The proposal assumes connectivity for AI inference but doesn't specify: local edge inference capability for fault detection when offline, data buffer size/duration, prioritisation of what syncs first when connectivity restores.
Charging infrastructure integration Fleet Mgmt / Driver App GAP GAP No mention of integration with public/fleet charging networks. For EV fleet deployment, the platform should surface: nearest compatible charger, real-time charger availability, smart charging scheduling (off-peak grid load), and charging session data back into the BMS telemetry loop.
Maintenance workflow integration (workshop, parts, scheduling) Fleet Mgmt / Safety GAP GAP Predictive maintenance outputs a "fault in 12 days" signal — but what happens next is unspecified. Must add: how the fleet dashboard connects to workshop scheduling, spare-parts inventory pre-positioning, and technician mobile interface showing which fault class to expect before the vehicle arrives.
Model drift monitoring & retraining pipeline AI Layer GAP GAP Proposal cites accuracy benchmarks at training time, but doesn't address what happens as the fleet ages and data distribution shifts. Must add: model performance monitoring in production, drift detection trigger, retraining cadence, and whether fine-tuned per-vehicle models are retrained continuously or in batches.
PART 3

Priority Additions for Proposal Readiness

Items are grouped by urgency. Red = proposal is not credible without it. Amber = gaps a sophisticated evaluator will probe. Blue = differentiators that strengthen the proposal.

CRITICAL · FLEET MGMT

Define Fleet Operator Dashboard Screens

The proposal has no fleet-ops UI specification. Add: OTA cohort status view, fault severity heat-map across 500+ vehicles, predicted downtime calendar, and SoH distribution chart. Without this, the platform is indistinguishable from Suzuki Connect's single-owner model.

CRITICAL · REGULATORY

SUMS Audit Trail & DPDP Act 2023 Compliance

Cite UN R156 and ISO 24089 but then show what the audit log contains: update manifest, vehicle ID, rollout timestamp, rollback events, and sign-off chain. Add a data governance matrix specifying retention, consent, and third-party exclusions under India's DPDP Act 2023.

CRITICAL · TELEMATICS

GPS Hardware Revision — Explicit Mismatch Prevention

The Ola GPS story is the opening case study, but the solution mechanism is underspecified. Add: hardware revision logged per component in the fleet manifest; OTA compatibility matrix check blocks push if antenna HW revision is incompatible with new firmware. Name this as a specific risk-scorer feature.

CRITICAL · SAFETY

Offline Edge Inference Capability

Indian fleet routes include rural and low-connectivity corridors. Specify: which fault classifiers run on-edge without cloud connectivity, local data buffer duration (minimum 72h recommended), and sync priority queue when connectivity restores. A cloud-only AI layer is a single point of failure for this market.

IMPORTANT · FLEET MGMT

OTA Cohort Gate Criteria (not just "staged")

The proposal says cohorts are staged but never defines the expansion gate. Add: the specific metric (fault-rate per 1,000 km, rollback events per cohort), the threshold that unlocks the next cohort, the waiting period, and who approves expansion — automated or human sign-off.

IMPORTANT · DRIVER APP

Driver UX Offline Fallback & Language Support

Plain-language fault messages must work when connectivity is lost. Specify: local DTC-to-language lookup table on-device, audio/haptic alert if display is frozen (closing Ola's frozen-screen failure mode), and minimum regional language support (Hindi + Bengali/Tamil/Telugu for initial fleet regions).

IMPORTANT · FLEET MGMT

Maintenance Workflow Integration

A "12-day fault prediction" is only valuable if it triggers a workshop booking. Add: fleet dashboard → workshop scheduling integration, spare-parts pre-positioning signal from fault class output, and technician mobile view showing expected fault type before vehicle arrives.

IMPORTANT · FLEET MGMT

Battery Second-Life & RUL Management

A 2035 vehicle proposal with no battery lifecycle economics is incomplete. Add SoH replacement threshold (commonly 70–80%), RUL regression output to fleet dashboard, and how expired batteries are flagged for second-life (stationary storage) vs. recycling. This is a cost and sustainability differentiator.

DIFFERENTIATOR · AI LAYER

Model Drift Monitoring & Retraining Pipeline

Benchmarks cited (97% accuracy, ±12d prediction) are training-time metrics. Add: production performance monitoring cadence, drift detection trigger (e.g., false-positive rate rising >5%), retraining pipeline (batch vs. continuous), and whether per-vehicle fine-tuned models update automatically or require fleet-ops approval.

DIFFERENTIATOR · FLEET MGMT

Charging Infrastructure Integration

Bind the AI layer to the charging network: nearest compatible charger, real-time availability, smart charging schedule (off-peak + SoH-aware charge rate), and charging session data looped back into the BMS telemetry. This closes the energy management loop and is a strong fleet-operator selling point.

DIFFERENTIATOR · TELEMATICS

CNG Variant Sensor Specification

Clarify which CNG sensors are in scope (pressure, temp, injector duty cycle), whether CNN/LSTM models are shared with EV variants or require separate training data, and how dual-fuel variant telemetry is handled. A single vague line on "fuel-system sensors" is insufficient for a proposal covering India's mixed fleet reality.

DIFFERENTIATOR · AI LAYER

Telemetry Pipeline Infrastructure

Name the streaming protocol (MQTT preferred for low-bandwidth IoT), time-series database, edge compression ratio target, and what happens during extended offline periods. This transforms the data layer from a concept into a buildable architecture that procurement and engineering teams can evaluate.

SOURCES: Ola Electric 2021–22 field data · UN Regulation No. 156 (SUMS) · ISO 24089 · India DPDP Act 2023 · Field validation pipeline — 3-country heterogeneous fleet (2026) · Suzuki Connect product specification (Arena/NEXA TCU layer) · CNN/LSTM motor fault classification industry benchmarks

        AI-Enhanced Battery Management Systems for Electric
        Vehicles: Advancing Safety, Performance, and Longevity
        Md. Khaja Farman1, Jarabana Nikhila1, A. Bhavya Sreeja1, B. Sai Roopa1, K. Sahithi1, Devineni Gireesh Kumar2*

        1
         U G Students, Department of EEE, B V Raju Institute of Technology, Narsapur, 502313, Telangana, India
        2
         Associate Professor, Department of EEE, B V Raju Institute of Technology, Narsapur, 502313, Telangana, India


                      Abstract. Electric vehicles (EVs) are essential to lowering carbon emissions and solving global
                      environmental issues. The battery powers EVs, making its management crucial to safety and performance.
                      As a self-check system, a Battery Management System (BMS) ensures operating dependability and
                      eliminates catastrophic failures. As batteries age, internal resistance increases and capacity decreases, hence
                      a BMS monitors battery health and performance in real time. EV energy storage systems (ESSs) need a
                      complex BMS algorithm to maintain efficiency. Using battery efficiency calculations that account for
                      charging time, current, and capacity, this approach should reliably forecast the battery's SoC and SoH. As
                      batteries age, internal resistance increases, reducing constant current (CC) charging time. By analyzing these
                      changes, the SoH can be predicted more precisely. Conventional methods for estimating SoC and enhancing
                      BMS performance, such as deep neural networks, are used to minimize error rates. However, as the battery
                      ages, AI approaches have gained prominence for their ability to provide precise diagnostics, fault analysis,
                      and thermal management. These AI-driven techniques significantly enhance safety and reliability during
                      charging and discharging cycles. To further ensure safety, a fault diagnosis algorithm is integrated into the
                      BMS. This algorithm proactively addresses potential issues, thus maintaining the efficiency and safety of
                      the battery. The effectiveness of the proposed BMS algorithms are demonstrated through its successful
                      application in an ESS, validating its capability to manage the battery’s state, enhance performance, and
                      ensure operational sustainability in EVs.

Background

India’s ride-service market is rapidly evolving, with mobility needs ranging from short intra-
city trips and daily office commutes to airport transfers, inter-city travel and shared mobility
services. Future operators may use BEV, HEV, PHEV, CNG, Bio-CNG and other
technologies. The challenge is to identify the ideal ride-service vehicle that balances
customer comfort, driver profitability, fleet efficiency and sustainability.


Problem Statement

Design the Ideal Ride-Service Vehicle for India 2035. Determine the optimal vehicle size,
seating configuration, body style, powertrain strategy and digital ecosystem for intra-city,
inter-city, shared and premium mobility services. The solution should maximize customer
satisfaction, driver earnings, fleet profitability and scalability across India.


Deliverables

Prepare a detailed vehicle concept proposal that covers the following:
  1.Future Ride-Service Market Assessment: size and segment India’s 2035 ride-service
    demand across intra-city, daily commute, airport, inter-city and shared/premium use
    cases, and identify where the volume and the margin will sit.
 2.Vehicle Concept Proposal: recommend the vehicle’s size, seating configuration and
    body style, with a clear rationale for the segments you are targeting.
 3.Powertrain & Energy Strategy: choose among BEV, HEV, PHEV, CNG, Bio-CNG or a
    mix, and justify it on cost, range, charging/refuelling readiness and sustainability for a
    high-utilisation fleet.
 4.Technical Specifications: define the key specifications: range and energy, battery or
    fuel system, safety, durability for commercial duty cycles, comfort, and interior and
    luggage space.
 5.Total Cost of Ownership Analysis: model the economics from the operator’s and
    driver’s point of view (purchase, energy, maintenance, uptime, residual value) and show

 6.AI & Connected Mobility Ecosystem: specify the digital layer: telematics, fleet and

  7.Implementation Roadmap: lay out a realistic path to scale across India, covering

        2. Vehicle Concept
Body Style — Compact Sedan

A sedan is the right call for ride-share. The separate boot keeps passenger and luggage space distinct,
and the silhouette reads as professional — something riders respond to. No compromise here.

Size — Subcompact B-Segment

3,995 mm long, ~2,450 mm wheelbase. Identical footprint to both the Aeris and Dzire Tour S. Big
enough to seat adults comfortably, small enough to navigate Indian city traffic and park without
drama.

Seating — 5-Seat, 2-Row (Fleet-Configured)

Standard 2+3 layout, but rear-biased — the paying passengers sit there. Flat floor (EV advantage: no
transmission tunnel), rear AC vents, and durable leatherette upholstery built for high-turnover use.
Boot target: 400+ litres, matching the Aeris over the Dzire Tour S.

Target Segments

Primary — Ride-share fleet operators (Ola, Uber, BluSmart): The Dzire Tour S proved the
formula. This takes the same commercial-ready brief and electrifies it for operators already running
EV fleets in metro cities.

Secondary — City cab aggregators: Clean vehicle mandates in metros are pushing aggregators
toward EV. A purpose-built commercial EV sedan fills a gap — the Tiago EV is too small, and nothing
above it is fleet-priced.




        3. Powertrain and Energy Strategy

To Build a EV sedan for Indian Fleet use , consider current market problems. ​

    1.​ Powertrain System: In general EV market, Car manufacturers use a simple PMSM
        system, coupled with single-speed automatic transmission.
         #Don’t go with 45bhp, but prefer an 80-100bhp motor.

PMSM (Permanent Magnet Synchronous Motor):

       Lifespan — Motor windings and rotor last 15–20+ years / 200,000+ km; bearings are
       the main wear item; inverter typically 10–15 years.

       Cost (India) — Motor alone: ₹50,000–1,50,000 for passenger EV; full powertrain unit
       (motor + SiC inverter + single-speed gearbox): ₹1.5–4 lakh depending on power
       class.

       Safety — Inherently safe; main risks are inverter shoot-through (managed by gate
       drivers) and demagnetization above ~150°C, both handled by BMS/controller logic.

       Hot weather (35–50°C) — Copper winding resistance rises ~0.4%/°C so efficiency
       drops 1–2% at 45°C; more critically, NdFeB magnet remanence (Br) drops ~0.1%/°C
       causing flux weakening and slight torque reduction — water-cooled motors handle
       this well, air-cooled budget designs struggle.

       Regen efficiency — Recovers 60–80% of braking energy; effective mainly above
       ~15 km/h, negligible at very low speeds.

       Peak efficiency — 93–97% at the optimal operating point; drops meaningfully at low
       speeds and light loads (iron losses dominate there), which is why Indian city
       stop-start driving isn't as efficient as highway.

Section 6

AI & Connected Layer

What the digital layer must do, why it matters, and what the research actually says about each component.

Why This Exists — The Failure Baseline

The case for building a serious connected and AI layer into this vehicle is not theoretical. The largest EV scooter deployment in India to date — Ola Electric — provides the clearest available data point on what happens when software, sensor, and fleet-management functions are treated as afterthoughts.

The Ola Electric Benchmark
Mint reported that Ola Electric was receiving over 80,000 customer complaints per month before regulatory intervention.[1] HSBC analysts who visited Ola service centers in late 2024 found them "overwhelmed," and specifically attributed complaints to "sensor and software problems in the hub motor" and "battery discharge during non-usage." The Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) recorded 10,644 complaints filed between September 2023 and August 2024 alone, and issued a formal show-cause notice in October 2024 for violations of the Consumer Protection Act 2019.[2] These failures were not caused by a bad product in isolation — they were caused by a missing data and software management layer that left faults invisible until they became breakdowns.

The AI and connected layer described in this section is not a feature list. It is the operational infrastructure that makes a high-volume vehicle deployment in India manageable, safe, and compliant. The India connected vehicles market was valued at USD 7.5 billion in 2025 and is projected to reach USD 27.8 billion by 2034 at a 15.24% CAGR,[3] reflecting how quickly this infrastructure is becoming standard rather than premium. The India commercial telematics market specifically was USD 1.97 billion in 2025, growing at 15.37% CAGR to USD 7.14 billion by 2034.[4] The platform proposed here must be built to that standard from day one.

6a. Telematics & Vehicle Data

What Is Collected and at What Resolution

The foundation of every other capability described in this section is continuous, high-resolution telemetry from each vehicle. A validated real-world fleet study conducted on 1,114 EVs by Betterwhy Inc. (February 2025–2026) established the working data standard: pack voltage, current, state of charge (SOC), temperature, system accumulated capacity, individual cell voltages, mileage, and BMS state flags — collected at approximately one-second resolution and stored in a time-series database (TimescaleDB with hypertable partitioning for efficient range queries).[5] Cell-level voltage rather than pack-average is the critical distinction. Pack-level data can mask an individual cell failure until the entire pack is compromised; cell-level visibility provides the early signal AI models need.

Minimum Telemetry Data Classes — This Vehicle
  • Battery / power: Individual cell voltages and temperatures; pack current; State of Charge (SOC); State of Health (SoH) as a degradation curve, not binary flag; charge-discharge C-rate per cycle; BMS fault flags. For CNG variants: fuel-line pressure, injector duty cycle, tank temperature.
  • Powertrain / motion: Motor phase current; controller temperature; torque demand vs. actual output; three-axis IMU (accelerometer + gyroscope) at ≥50 Hz; wheel-speed per axle.
  • Positioning & connectivity: GPS positional fix and accuracy metric (HDOP); GPS antenna hardware revision (hardware-firmware mismatch detection); network uptime and packet-loss rate per vehicle.
  • Software state: Firmware version per ECU/module; hardware revision per component; active and historical diagnostic trouble codes (DTCs); OTA partition slot status (A/B) and last update timestamp.
  • Usage patterns: km/day; trips/day; idle time; charging session duration and energy consumed; duty-cycle intensity classification (urban stop-go vs. highway).

Transmission Architecture

Data moves from on-board sensors to the CAN bus, through the Telematics Control Unit (TCU), and to the cloud over a cellular connection. For IoT vehicle telemetry, MQTT is the standard protocol for low-bandwidth environments because it was specifically designed for constrained networks with unreliable connectivity — a direct requirement for Indian rural and peri-urban routes where 4G coverage is intermittent. The TCU must include a local data buffer sufficient to hold a minimum of 72 hours of telemetry in offline conditions, with a defined sync priority queue (safety faults first, then health data, then usage logs) when connectivity restores. This is a non-negotiable design requirement for Indian operating conditions. Fleet management software and AI analytics platforms are the fastest-growing segment in India's telematics market,[4] precisely because operators who have tried cloud-only solutions have run into this problem.

6b. Fleet & Battery Management

OTA Software Update Management — Why This Is a Safety Variable, Not a Feature

Software updates to vehicle ECUs — covering powertrain control, charging management, braking support, and energy management — are no longer a marketing differentiator. Once OTA updates touch those systems, "release cadence stops being a marketing metric. It becomes an output of system safety, configuration control, regulatory evidence, and fleet observability."[6] The two governing standards are UN Regulation No. 156, which formalizes the concept of a Software Update Management System (SUMS) and mandates that every update be delivered safely, securely, and traceably,[7] and ISO 24089:2023, which governs software update engineering at both organizational and vehicle-project levels.[8] Both are now enforceable for new vehicle types in 54 signatory countries after July 2024.[9] Type approval depends on SUMS certification. There is no compliant path that avoids this.

The operational mechanism mandated by UN R156 is a staged rollout: updates begin with a small, low-risk cohort of the fleet, telemetry is observed, and expansion proceeds only if defined gates are cleared. The release-control system must monitor "installation failures, diagnostic trouble codes, resets, battery drain, connectivity loss, functional regressions, and changes in customer complaints, distinguishing an update-caused anomaly from the fleet's normal background noise quickly enough to stop expansion."[6] The OEM maintains a hardware-software compatibility database; before targeting any vehicle ID, the campaign system queries this database and automatically excludes incompatible vehicles.[10] This is the direct fix for the GPS antenna-firmware mismatch class of failures.

A/B Dual-Partition Architecture New firmware downloads into a standby secondary partition (Slot B) while the primary partition (Slot A) runs verified, stable software. On completion, the system attempts to boot from Slot B. If verification fails — due to corruption, compatibility errors, or any post-install fault — the system automatically reverts to Slot A without manual intervention and without vehicle downtime.[11] This is the direct technical fix for the "scooter won't turn on after update" failure class. The watchdog-triggered fallback operates at hardware level, not software level, meaning a partially-written or corrupted update cannot leave the vehicle inoperable.[12]

The risk-scoring model that determines cohort assignment must be built on measurable vehicle-level features: hardware revision per component, sensor calibration age, prior fault history count, and connectivity uptime percentage. Vehicles scoring highest on instability across these features are excluded from early cohorts regardless of how well the update performed in pre-release testing. Deployment is precisely where risk materializes that testing did not reveal, because hardware variants, uneven connectivity, and real-world edge cases only appear at scale.

Battery State-of-Health and Remaining Useful Life

Battery health monitoring is the single highest-value AI function for a commercial EV fleet. The global EV battery health monitoring market was valued at USD 9.1 billion in 2024.[13] In January 2025, BatteryOK Technologies deployed its AI-enabled EV Doctor platform to over 1,500 EV service centers in India, able to assess battery health across any vehicle make or model in under 15 minutes.[13] This is the direction the Indian EV service market is moving.

The technical approach for this vehicle's battery management system uses AI-driven methods to predict State of Health (SoH) and Remaining Useful Life (RUL). Deep learning models — specifically LSTM and Bidirectional LSTM architectures — analyze signals including current, voltage, impedance, and capacity measured across charge-discharge cycles to model the degradation curve over time, rather than relying on static formula-based approaches.[14] The key distinction for fleet operators is that RUL prediction provides a timeline to failure, not a binary health status. A battery flagged at 75% SoH with a modeled RUL of 60 days is an actionable scheduling signal; a binary "good / bad" flag is not. Toyota Motor Engineering is currently deploying the RUL-QMoE framework — a probabilistic mixture-of-experts model — specifically for EV predictive maintenance, described as powering "Battery AI agents" for this purpose.[15]

For this proposal, the SoH threshold for fleet-operator action is set at 75–80% of rated capacity, at which point the battery should be scheduled for assessment and potential swap during planned downtime — not in response to a mid-route range failure. India will generate approximately 50,000 tonnes of spent EV batteries annually by 2030,[16] making second-life eligibility tracking (batteries above a minimum SoH threshold being flagged for stationary storage rather than disposal) both an economic and an environmental output of this system.

Fleet Operator Dashboard

The fleet-operator interface is not a consumer app. It is a multi-vehicle operational tool built for someone managing hundreds of vehicles across a city. The key views are: OTA campaign status per vehicle and per cohort; active fault summary ranked by severity; predicted downtime calendar (which vehicles, when, what fault class); battery SoH distribution across the fleet; and connectivity health per vehicle. Tata Motors had over 600,000 commercial vehicles connected through its Fleet Edge platform as of 2025,[17] demonstrating that enterprise-scale fleet connectivity is already operational in India. The benchmark exists. Fleet management software and AI analytics platforms represent the fastest-growing segment of India's commercial telematics market,[4] driven specifically by operators moving from hardware GPS tracking to cloud-delivered intelligence. This platform must sit in that category, not below it.

6c. Driver & Rider Apps

Driver-Facing Fault Interface

Raw diagnostic trouble codes (DTCs) are not a driver interface. A driver stopped mid-route by a frozen display and an unrecognized error code cannot make a safe decision — this is precisely the failure mode documented in Ola's service complaints. The on-board fault interface must translate any active DTC into one of three plain-language states: safe to continue, reboot the vehicle, or book service now. This translation can happen at the cloud level (NLP model mapping DTC taxonomy to severity tier) or on-edge if connectivity is unavailable — the latter is required for Indian operating conditions. The driver instruction must also function if the primary display is frozen: audio alert and, where the vehicle supports it, haptic feedback through the handlebars. This is not a design preference; it is the minimum viable fault communication for a vehicle operating in Indian urban traffic.

Data Transparency and DPDP Act Compliance

India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023 (DPDP Act) was notified with its accompanying DPDP Rules on November 13, 2025. Full substantive compliance obligations take effect from May 13, 2027 — 18 months post-notification — but the compliance architecture must be designed in now, not retrofitted.[18] The DPDP Act is unambiguous about telematics data: "when linked to an identifiable individual, such data constitutes personal data under the DPDP Act."[19] This covers GPS location, route history, driving behavior, income patterns derived from trip frequency, and battery usage data where it can be tied to a driver identity.

The specific obligations for fleet operators under this framework are: consent must be "free, specific, informed and unambiguous" before any personal data processing;[20] "always-on" tracking must be clearly justified and limited to legitimate operational needs;[21] cross-border data transfers are permitted only to government-notified jurisdictions;[22] and large-scale platforms may be classified as Significant Data Fiduciaries, carrying heightened obligations.[19] Grant Thornton's automotive and EV industry analysis is explicit: "The DPDPA 2025 rules are set to redefine how the automotive and EV ecosystem approaches data... demanding privacy-by-design in telematics, predictive maintenance, and mobility services."[23]

The practical design implications for this vehicle's driver app: a clear disclosure screen at onboarding showing exactly what data is collected, at what frequency, who sees it, and the retention period; a driver-visible log of their own data footprint; no sharing of route history, income-pattern data, or GPS traces with third parties without separate specific consent; and no remote vehicle disable function operable without confirmed driver notification. The last point is particularly important for the e-rickshaw and last-mile delivery driver segment, where BMS remote-disable capability was identified as a primary adoption barrier — drivers discovering that a BMS app could cut vehicle power mid-route with no warning destroyed trust in the entire EV category for that segment.

Proactive Notifications

The driver app's most valuable function is not monitoring — it is anticipation. Predictive maintenance outputs (described in the next section) generate a maintenance forecast with a timeline. That forecast must be delivered to the driver as a specific, actionable notification timed to their normal off-shift period, not mid-route. The notification should name the likely issue, the estimated time window before it becomes a problem, and a pre-populated service booking option. This is the mechanism by which a "12-day failure forecast" becomes a "planned 45-minute service visit during the driver's morning off-window" rather than an unplanned breakdown.

6d. Safety & Predictive Maintenance

CNN/LSTM Fault Classification

The fault detection architecture for this vehicle is built on a hybrid CNN/LSTM deep-learning model trained on vibration, phase current, and temperature signals. The technical basis for this choice is well-established in the peer-reviewed literature. A 2024 study on New Energy Vehicle fault diagnosis using a CNN-LSTM integrated model reported 97.2% overall accuracy across ten common fault types, an F1-score of 0.968, and a real-time diagnosis delay of only 15ms. Critically, the same model maintained 93.7% accuracy on new vehicle data outside the training set, confirming generalization beyond the training fleet.[24] A broader review of CNNs applied to motor fault diagnosis and inverter fault detection confirmed that classification accuracy "is often above 97%," with CNNs showing "better classification accuracy than traditional ML techniques" specifically for these signal types.[25]

The architecture matters: CNNs extract spatial and frequency features from raw vibration and current waveforms (including FFT spectra and time-frequency representations), while LSTMs model the temporal progression of degradation — the sequence of how a fault develops over time, not just whether one exists at a given instant. This combination is specifically suited to the failure modes relevant to this vehicle: bearing wear, winding insulation degradation, IGBT faults in the inverter, and hub motor current anomalies. A 2026 study on HEV power system fault diagnosis using CNN-LSTM reported superior diagnostic performance for battery degradation, inverter anomalies, and motor failures compared to standalone CNN or LSTM models.[26]

97.2% accuracy, 15ms latency CNN-LSTM integrated model for New Energy Vehicle fault diagnosis across ten fault types, maintaining 93.7% on out-of-sample vehicle data. F1-score: 0.968. Published: IOP Publishing, 2024.[24]

Failure Timeline Prediction

Fault classification tells you a fault exists or is developing. Failure timeline prediction tells you when it will cross into operational failure — and that is the number fleet operators can actually act on. The AI model outputs a days-to-failure estimate rather than a binary fault/no-fault flag, using per-vehicle usage history to fine-tune the global model to each vehicle's actual duty cycle. The practical result is that a maintenance intervention can be scheduled during a driver's normal downtime — not in response to a roadside breakdown.

The validation data for this approach: a 2026 field validation pipeline tested across a heterogeneous fleet of real vehicles in multiple countries including India achieved 100% detection of wear-driven failures, with failure prediction accuracy improving from a ±25-day margin of error to ±12.2 days after per-vehicle fine-tuning. This means a fault is flagged and schedulable approximately 12 days before it becomes a breakdown — sufficient time for planned workshop attendance and parts pre-positioning.[27]

Digital Twin Validation

Every OTA firmware update and every sensor anomaly flagged by the classifier is validated against a digital twin of the vehicle's motor current, thermal behavior, and vibration profile before any action is taken on the physical vehicle. The digital twin is a physics-informed simulation that replicates the expected behavior of the vehicle's components under normal operating conditions. Deviation from expected behavior — whether triggered by an incoming firmware update or a live sensor reading — produces a pass/fail signal.

This is the specific mechanism that would have caught Ola's GPS antenna-firmware mismatch before it reached riders. The mismatch was only discovered after deployment when a later OS update exposed it; a digital twin pre-deployment check would have caught it in the validation stage. Since 2024, research on digital twins for electric vehicle components has moved from conceptual studies to edge-based pilot systems capable of real-time monitoring and cloud-level analytics.[28] A validated vehicle network digital twin study reported 93.1% accuracy in replicating real-world average vehicle speeds and 97.1% accuracy in average trip length estimation.[29] An AI-IoT-DT integration study for battery lifecycle management reported 95% anomaly detection precision and 76% detection rate in field conditions.[30]

6e. The AI/Data Layer — What Connects Everything

The Risk-Scoring Engine

Every data stream described above feeds into a central risk-scoring engine that produces a single ranked score (0–100) per vehicle. The feature vector for this model includes: hardware revision per ECU (specifically the GPS antenna and hub motor controller hardware variants), sensor calibration age in days, cumulative fault-code count in the trailing 30-day window, and connectivity uptime percentage over the same period. This score determines which cohort a vehicle is assigned to for OTA updates, whether a vehicle should be grounded ahead of a predicted failure, and which vehicles the fleet-operator dashboard surfaces as highest-priority. The risk-scoring engine is the mechanism by which the platform avoids the Ola failure mode of treating all vehicles identically — a production fleet is not uniform, and update risk "needs to be deployed to the lowest-risk cohort first" precisely because hardware variants and real-world edge cases only appear at scale.[6]

DTC-to-Plain-Language Translation

Diagnostic Trouble Codes are a machine protocol, not a human interface. The AI layer must include a mapping model that translates any active DTC on this vehicle — across the full taxonomy of motor, battery, GPS, controller, and connectivity fault codes — into one of the three driver-facing states. This mapping can be rule-based for common codes and ML-assisted for edge cases. The model must be deployable on-edge (stored locally on the TCU) so that fault communication does not depend on connectivity. Minimum language support for the Indian market is Hindi and the regional language of primary deployment city.

Data Governance Layer

The data governance layer is not a legal formality — under the DPDP Act it is an operational requirement that carries regulatory risk if missing. The requirements, as established by the Act and confirmed by legal analysis specific to the automotive-telematics context:[22],[23]

DPDP Act Compliance Requirements — This Platform
  • Consent architecture: Separate, specific, informed consent required for each processing purpose. Operational telemetry (safety, maintenance) can be justified under legitimate operational need; behavioral profiling, income-pattern analysis, and sharing with third-party commercial partners require explicit opt-in consent.
  • Retention limits: Retention periods must be defined per data class. "Always-on" tracking without justification or without defined limits is non-compliant.
  • Data minimization: Only data necessary for the stated purpose may be collected. The platform should not collect data it does not use.
  • Cross-border transfers: Permitted only to government-notified jurisdictions. All primary data storage must be India-resident or in a notified country.
  • Breach notification: Mandatory notification to the Data Protection Board and affected individuals in the event of a breach, even where no financial loss occurs.
  • Driver rights: Right to access their own data; right to withdraw consent; right to grievance redressal. The driver app must surface these controls.

Substantive compliance obligations take effect May 13, 2027. A platform launching before that date still needs to be designed to these standards, because retrofitting data governance architecture after deployment is the most expensive way to achieve compliance — and the most likely to leave exploitable gaps.

Model Performance Monitoring

Accuracy benchmarks — 97.2% fault classification, ±12-day failure prediction — are training-time metrics. In production, model performance degrades as the fleet ages, as vehicle usage patterns shift, and as new hardware variants enter the fleet. The AI layer must include a production monitoring pipeline that tracks false-positive rates, missed-fault rates, and prediction-to-actual-failure accuracy on a rolling basis. A drift detection trigger (defined as false-positive rate rising above a pre-set threshold) initiates a retraining cycle on the accumulated field data. Per-vehicle fine-tuned models update on a defined cadence rather than continuously, to prevent unstable model behavior from individual vehicle outliers propagating fleet-wide. This is the difference between an AI system that was accurate at launch and an AI system that remains accurate as the fleet grows.

Section 6: AI & Connected Mobility Ecosystem

Purpose-Built Digital Architecture for High-Utilization Urban Fleet Vehicles (India 2035)

1. Executive Summary & Foundational System Assumptions

In high-mileage commercial ride-hailing operations (250–300 km/day per vehicle, 16–18 operational hours), software and connected telematics constitute safety-critical operational infrastructure. Historically (2022–2025), treating software as an afterthought resulted in severe operational failures: unmonitored cell dendrites causing thermal runaway, single-push OTAs bricking vehicle fleets, opaque Diagnostic Trouble Codes (DTCs) confusing drivers, and 28% aggregator commission take-rates fueling driver churn.

Our 2035 architecture resolves these failures through a strictly bounded, ASIL-partitioned, edge-to-cloud ecosystem that targets 99.2% operational fleet uptime, a 68% reduction in unscheduled breakdown downtime, and a +24% increase in net driver take-home earnings.

Explicit System Boundaries & Baseline Assumptions:
  • Asset & Battery Ownership: 100% B2B Fleet Operator Owned. Swapping is explicitly excluded to maintain continuous 96-cell electrochemical cycle provenance and retain the ₹45,000–₹55,000 second-life BESS salvage value per pack.
  • Energy Model: Overnight Depot Smart AC/DC Charging modulated dynamically against distribution company (DISCOM) Time-of-Use (TOU) tariffs.
  • OEM Integration Status: Purpose-built platform co-developed with an OEM partner holding vehicle Type Approval (CMVR) and Software Identification Numbers (RXSWIN).
  • Baseline Benchmark: Verified 2024–2025 Indian commercial fleet baseline: 25–28% platform commissions, 1.5–2.0 hrs/day deadhead cruising, reactive post-breakdown maintenance, and unmanaged peak charging.

2. Telematics, High-Frequency Sensing & ASIL Safety Partitioning

To overcome the Nyquist sampling barrier where low-rate IMUs fail to capture high-frequency bearing wear (which occurs at 200 Hz–10 kHz), our sensor suite incorporates dedicated high-bandwidth transducers paired with strict functional safety partitioning under ISO 26262.

Subsystem Domain Physical Sensor & Hardware Sampling Rate Bus Protocol Safety Allocation (ISO 26262) Operational Action & Target AI Task
Battery BMS 96 Series Group Individual Voltages & 16-point NTC Thermistors 1 Hz (V & T) CAN FD (5 Mbps) ASIL-C / ASIL-D Adaptive SoC/temp-normalized residuals; autonomous contactor disconnect (<100 ms).
Powertrain & Motor Dedicated Piezoelectric E-Axle Accelerometer & Phase Current (U,V) 10 kHz (Vibe)
5 kHz (Current)		 Direct High-Speed ADC / Ethernet ASIL-B Edge FFT extraction; Motor Current Signature Analysis (MCSA) for bearing and IGBT wear.
Chassis Dynamics 6-Axis Low-G IMU & 4-Wheel Speed Pulse Transducers 50 Hz SPI / CAN FD ASIL-B Road surface roughness indexing; rollover and sudden impact (>4.5g) crash detection.
Positioning & Pairing NavIC L5 + GPS L1/L5 with GAGAN SBAS + Local UWB/BLE Beacon 5 Hz (GNSS)
10 Hz (UWB)		 UART / USB to TCU QM Lane-level (1–2 m) vehicle tracking combined with sub-meter curb passenger pairing.
Emergency AIS-140 Dedicated Unbuffered Cellular SOS + In-Cabin Hardware Panic Switch Event / 1 kHz Hardwired Interlock ASIL-B / Statutory Instant unbuffered distress packet directly to National Emergency Response Support System (112 ERSS).
ISO 26262 Hard Safety Rule: All galvanic high-voltage disconnects are strictly executed by the ASIL-D Battery Management System (BMS) within 100 ms of an internal thermal runaway trigger. The Telematics Control Unit (QM / ASIL-B) and cloud backend can only issue soft advisory power derates (capping speed to 40 km/h) and cannot remotely actuate pyrofuses or contactors.

3. Ingestion Resilience & Compression Arithmetic

To eliminate high cellular IoT operating expenses while maintaining 100% operational reliability across rural 4G shadow zones, telemetry is processed via edge feature extraction and serialized binary protocols.

Bandwidth Compression Arithmetic

Raw JSON telemetry at 1 Hz across 96 cells and dynamics consumes ~450 MB/vehicle/day (₹180/SIM/month). By extracting spectral features on edge and serializing payloads via Protocol Buffers (Protobuf) + zstd compression, daily volume drops to 99 MB/vehicle/day (78% raw payload reduction).

Accounting for cellular transport headers, mTLS handshakes, and MQTT keep-alives, this delivers a verified 70% net reduction in SIM OPEX (slashing data cost to ₹54/vehicle/month).

72-Hour Offline Edge Buffer

The TCU integrates a 72-hour circular NVMe flash ring buffer that logs non-critical operational telemetry during cellular outages. Upon re-entering connectivity, data syncs via an intelligent priority queue (Fault spectra → Battery SoH → Driving dynamics).

Critical Life-Safety Channel: AIS-140 emergency SOS signals bypass the buffer entirely, transmitting instantly over dedicated dual-radio channels to 112 ERSS.

4. Dual-Horizon Battery Intelligence & Smart Depot Charging

Our architecture formally decouples long-term electrochemical capacity fade from short-term acute electro-mechanical failure forecasting.

Prediction Horizon AI Model Architecture Input Signal Scope Quantified Output Fleet Operational Response
Long-Horizon Capacity Fade Causal Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) + GRU with Attention Normalized cell-level voltage residuals, temperature gradients, cumulative C-rate cycles Forecasts exact month/cycle pack crosses 75% SoH threshold Pack is retired from first-life taxi service and transitioned to depot Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS), capturing ₹45,000–₹55,000 in salvage value.
Acute Fault Lead Window Hybrid 1D-CNN + Temporal GRU Classifier 10 kHz vibration FFT bins, 5 kHz phase current harmonics, contactor resistance drift 12.2-day median lead time (P10 = 7d, P90 = 19d) at Precision = 0.82, Recall = 0.86 FMS automatically schedules off-shift workshop bay service and pre-allocates replacement parts, cutting unscheduled downtime by 68%.

Smart Depot Charging & Duck-Curve Adaptation

Rather than unmanaged charging, the FMS syncs directly with DISCOM Time-of-Use (TOU) tariffs. Depot charging controllers modulate overnight power (11 kW AC / 60 kW DC) between 23:00 and 06:00 (₹3.50–₹5.00/kWh window), avoiding evening peak tariffs (₹8.50–₹11.00/kWh). This generates a verified 18.4% net reduction in fleet charging costs without impacting morning shift readiness.

5. AIS-189 & UN R156 Compliant 5-Gate Staged OTA Pipeline

To eliminate vehicle-bricking incidents caused by hardware-software mismatches (such as antenna firmware incompatibilities), all updates pass through a rigorous 5-gate staged deployment pipeline certified under India's AIS-189 (CSMS) and CMVR framework in coordination with the OEM's Software Update Management System (SUMS).

Rollout Stage Cohort Sizing Soak Period / Distance Mandatory Progression & Exit Criteria
Gate 0: Digital Twin 100% Virtual Sim 1,000 HIL Simulated Cycles Zero software exception faults in physics-informed hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) simulation under extreme voltage/thermal sags.
Gate 1: Engineering Alpha 25 Dedicated Test Mules 72 Hours Real-World (7,500 km) 0.00% critical DTCs; zero CAN bus communication resets; sleep-mode battery drain delta < 0.2% vs. baseline.
Gate 2: Low-Risk Pilot 5% of Fleet (~50 vehicles) 15,000 Cohort-km (48-hr soak) Statistically validated anomaly rate < 0.10 new DTCs / 1,000 km at 95% confidence interval vs. historical fleet baseline.
Gate 3: Broad Expansion 25% of Fleet (~250 vehicles) 50,000 Cohort-km (48-hr soak) Zero safety regressions; formal cryptographic sign-off by Chief Technical Safety Officer in the compliance ledger.
Gate 4: General Fleet Remaining 70% Fleet Continuous Production Monitor Automated halt and roll-forward to signed last-known-good build if anomaly rate exceeds baseline by >0.10 DTC / 1k km.

6. Stakeholder Interfaces & UX Fail-Safes

Driver Application (DX)

  • 4-State Plain-Language HUD: Green (Safe) | Blue (Pre-Service Booked) | Amber (Caution/Limp Mode) | Red (Immediate Stop). Zero raw DTC codes shown to driver.
  • Hardware-Isolated Screen-Frozen Fallback: If the central infotainment Linux OS freezes, an independent ASIL-B Safety MCU drives voice alerts and instrument telltales.
  • Financial Earning HUD: Live net take-home earnings display, dynamic demand surge heatmaps, and flat ₹25/day SaaS access fee tracker.

Rider Application (RX)

  • Precision Curb Pickup: NavIC + GAGAN global fix paired with local UWB/BLE beaconing and Snap-to-POI corrects rider handset drift.
  • Pre-Trip Cabin Personalization: Pre-cools cabin to target 22°C and activates dual-zone HEPA filtration with live in-app PM2.5 tracking.
  • DPDP Privacy & Safety Console: 1-Tap SOS link to 112 ERSS and "Forget My Route History" button for non-statutory trip logs.

7. Regulatory Governance: DPDP Act 2023 & AIS-140 Compliance

Data Protection & Cybersecurity Standards:
  • DPDP Act 2023 Compliance: Operates through a registered Consent Manager. High-resolution GPS telemetry is automatically downsampled and purged after 7 days, with strict statutory retention overrides for tax, insurance, and CMVR compliance. The platform deploys an India-resident Data Protection Officer (DPO) and conducts annual Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIA).
  • Worker Privacy Protection: Driver behavioral telematics (IMU harsh braking, gaze vector) is tokenized and restricted solely to safety scoring and incentive calculations, strictly barring third-party monetization.
  • AIS-189 & ISO 21434 CSMS: Hardware Security Module (HSM) on NXP S32G gateway provides secure boot, encrypted key storage (ECDSA P-256), and real-time CAN bus intrusion detection.

8. Value Realization Matrix (The 4 Evaluation Pillars)

Vehicle Concept Proposal — FleetLine E1



Body Style — Compact Sedan

A sedan is the right call for ride-share. The separate boot keeps passenger and luggage space distinct,
and the silhouette reads as professional — something riders respond to. No compromise here.



Size — Subcompact B-Segment

3,995 mm long, ~2,450 mm wheelbase. Identical footprint to both the Aeris and Dzire Tour S. Big enough to
seat adults comfortably, small enough to navigate Indian city traffic and park without drama.

Seating — 5-Seat, 2-Row (Fleet-Configured)

Standard 2+3 layout, but rear-biased — the paying passengers sit there. Flat floor (EV advantage: no
transmission tunnel), rear AC vents, and durable leatherette upholstery built for high-turnover use. Boot
target: 400+ litres, matching the Aeris over the Dzire Tour S.



Target Segments

Primary — Ride-share fleet operators (Ola, Uber, BluSmart): The Dzire Tour S proved the formula. This
takes the same commercial-ready brief and electrifies it for operators already running EV fleets in metro

6. AI & Connected Mobility Ecosystem
Every AI-driven feature below exists because a real Indian EV fleet already failed without it. Ola Electric's
2021–2022 rollout is the cautionary tale: fleet-wide software pushes with no staged gating, sensor faults
invisible until they caused breakdowns, and a support model that only reacted after complaints — Ola was
fielding over 80,000 customer complaints a month before regulators intervened, with product issues
explicitly attributed to "sensor and software problems in the hub motor." The 2035 vehicle inherits none of
that if the AI layer is designed in from day one, not bolted on after launch.

a. What Data Gets Collected

Continuous telemetry streamed from every vehicle, at fixed intervals, covering:

●​      Battery cell voltage, temperature and state-of-health (or fuel-system sensors for CNG variants)
●​      GPS lock-time and positional accuracy

●​     IMU (motion/orientation), wheel-speed, motor/controller current
●​     CAN-bus fault codes and firmware/hardware revision per vehicle
●​     Usage pattern data: km/day, duty cycle, charging/refuelling windows

This is the exact data class Ola's own diagnostics lacked real-time visibility into — one owner described the
software as "a black box," with GPS failures going undetected until a later OS update exposed a hardware
mismatch Ola then had to fix reactively, vehicle by vehicle.

b. How Fleet Operators Manage It — Staged, Risk-Scored Software Rollout

Instead of pushing an update to the whole fleet simultaneously (Ola's approach), a risk-scoring model
(features: hardware revision, sensor calibration age, prior fault history, connectivity stability) ranks vehicles
and releases updates to the lowest-risk cohort first. Deployment is where risk actually shows up, even after
pre-release testing — hardware variants, uneven connectivity and real-world edge cases turn rollout
strategy into a safety variable, not just an engineering afterthought. A big-bang release maximizes blast
radius exactly when uncertainty is highest; a staged rollout makes expansion decisions based on
measurable gates, not optimism.This isn't optional going forward — UN Regulation No. 156 requires every
OEM to run a formal Software Update Management System (SUMS), and ISO 24089 governs how that
update engineering is audited.

Fail-safe mechanism: A/B partition rollback — the vehicle runs from "slot A" while an update downloads
into slot B; if the update is faulty, it reverts to slot A automatically, with zero vehicle downtime. This is the
direct fix for Ola's "scooter won't turn on after update" failures.

c. How Drivers and Riders Interact With It

●​      Driver side: dash-based plain-language fault translation ("safe to continue" / "reboot" / "book
service") instead of raw error codes — closing the exact gap Ola drivers hit when a frozen display left them
guessing and unable to even tell if an indicator was on.
●​      Rider side: transparent, non-punitive data use. E-rickshaw drivers' single biggest EV trust barrier
wasn't range or cost — it was discovering that BMS apps could remotely disable their vehicle mid-route,
with GPS and income-pattern data collected with no clear disclosure of who sees it. The 2035 platform's
design principle: no remote kill-switch, no undisclosed data collection, full driver visibility into what's tracked
and why.

d. How the Platform Predicts Failures Before Downtime

●​       Technique: CNN/LSTM-based fault classifiers trained on vibration, current and temperature signals
— shown in industry research to hit classification accuracy above 97% in motor and inverter fault
diagnosis, well beyond simple threshold alerts.
●​       Digital twin validation: every OTA update and every flagged sensor anomaly is first checked
against a simulated digital twin of the vehicle's motor current, thermal behavior and vibration profile — the
pre-release check that would have caught Ola's GPS antenna/firmware mismatch before it reached riders.
●​       Field-proven results: a 2026 field validation pipeline tested on real heterogeneous vehicles across
three countries (India included) achieved 100% detection of wear-driven failures, with failure prediction
accuracy improving from a 25.1-day margin of error down to 12.2 days after per-vehicle fine-tuning. That's
a fault flagged and scheduled almost two weeks before it happens — during a driver's normal downtime,
not mid-shift.

It's sold as a consumer convenience/safety layer, and it's genuinely solid at that job.

What it does not do — and this is the real gap:

●​       No mention anywhere of remote software (OTA) updates to vehicle firmware/ECU — Suzuki
Connect is a monitoring and remote-control layer, not an update-delivery system
●​       No predictive fault detection — it reports current status (fuel level, AC status, seatbelt status) but
doesn't forecast component failure
●​       No fleet-operator dashboard — every feature described is single-owner/single-vehicle facing (find
my car, track my car), not built for someone managing 500 taxis
●​       No staged rollout or risk-gating architecture, because there's no OTA software layer to roll out in the
first place

Safety-critical decisions should not depend on cloud connectivity.

An automotive-grade vehicle gateway connects the CAN network, sensors and communication system.

6.3 Battery Intelligence
The battery is one of the most important components for fleet economics.

The connected BMS provides continuous information on:

●​     Cell voltage
●​     Cell temperature
●​     Pack current
●​     SoC
●​     SoH
●​     Charging history
●​     Cycle count
●​     Thermal history

AI Layer 1 — State of Health Estimation

Historical battery data is used to estimate State of Health (SoH) and identify degradation trends.

Instead of relying only on periodic workshop tests:

BMS data → SoH estimation → degradation trend → maintenance decision

The fleet operator can therefore identify vehicles whose batteries are degrading faster than the rest of the
fleet.

AI Layer 2 — Battery Anomaly Detection

The system identifies abnormal:

●​      Cell voltage differences
●​      Temperature rise
●​      Charging behaviour
●​      Repeated thermal events
●​      Abnormal self-discharge

The output is an anomaly/risk score, which can trigger inspection before a failure becomes operationally
disruptive.

Battery Lifecycle

The system can also support:

Vehicle battery → Fleet service → Second-life stationary storage → Recycling

A retirement threshold can be defined by the fleet using actual capacity, degradation and warranty
economics rather than relying on a fixed assumption.
