6.5 Smart Fleet Dispatch
Fleet AI should optimise more than simply sending the nearest vehicle.

The system considers:

●​     Vehicle location
●​     SoC
●​     Expected trip distance
●​     Current passenger demand
●​     Historical demand patterns
●​     Traffic
●​     Driver availability
●​     Charging requirements

Decision Logic

Demand + Location + SoC + Trip requirement + Driver availability

→ Vehicle assignment

Example

A vehicle may be physically closest to a booking but have low SoC and be unsuitable for a long
airport/inter-city trip.

The system can instead assign another vehicle with sufficient range while directing the low-SoC vehicle
toward shorter trips or charging.

Expected operational benefits

●​     Lower empty/deadhead kilometres
●​     Fewer range-related cancellations
●​     Better vehicle utilisation
●​     Better driver utilisation
●​     More predictable charging requirements

Target

Deadhead distance reduction: ~15%

Vehicle utilisation improvement: ~10%

These are proposed optimisation targets rather than guaranteed outcomes.

6.6 Smart Charging & Energy Management
Charging should be integrated with fleet scheduling rather than treated as a separate activity.

The system considers:

●​     Current SoC
●​     Next-shift requirement
●​     Expected trip demand
●​     Battery temperature
●​     Charger availability
●​     Electricity tariff
●​     Depot/grid constraints

Charging Optimisation

The system decides:

Which vehicle → When to charge → How much to charge

For example:

A vehicle returning late at night with sufficient SoC for its next trip does not necessarily need immediate
charging.

The system can schedule charging during a lower-tariff period while ensuring the vehicle reaches the
required SoC before its next shift.

Benefits

●​     Lower charging cost
●​     Reduced depot peak demand
●​     Better charger utilisation
●​     Reduced unnecessary high-SoC dwell time
●​     Improved fleet readiness

Target

15–18% reduction in charging energy cost as a fleet-level optimisation target.

6.7 Connectivity for Indian Operating
Conditions
A nationwide ride-service vehicle cannot assume uninterrupted connectivity.

The architecture therefore uses:

Primary Connectivity

4G LTE + 5G where available

4G remains the practical baseline for broad coverage, while 5G can be used where available for
higher-bandwidth services.

Communication Protocol

MQTT over TLS

MQTT is suitable for vehicle telemetry because it is lightweight and designed for connected devices
operating over variable networks.

Offline Operation

The vehicle gateway maintains a 72-hour local encrypted data buffer.

When connectivity is unavailable:

Vehicle → Local storage → Network restored → Secure synchronisation

Safety-critical events are prioritised.

This allows the vehicle to continue operating safely even when telemetry temporarily cannot reach the
cloud.

6.9 Safe OTA Software Updates
A connected commercial fleet requires controlled software deployment because a faulty update can affect
multiple vehicles simultaneously.

Four-stage OTA strategy

Gate 0 — Digital validation

↓

Gate 1 — Small pilot fleet

↓

Gate 2 — Limited fleet deployment

↓

Gate 3 — Expanded fleet deployment

↓

Gate 4 — Full fleet

At every stage:

Monitor → Compare baseline → Approve / Rollback

The update should be cryptographically signed and compatible with the vehicle's hardware/software
configuration.

If predefined safety or diagnostic thresholds are exceeded, deployment is automatically paused and the
previous stable version is restored.

This preserves the staged OTA and rollback architecture from the original concept.

control, and cloud connectivity to improve uptime, safety, and operational efficiency.

Technical Reference · EV Battery Chemistries

11 Battery Types Compared for Indian EV Conditions

Coverage: LFP · NMC · LMFP · NCA · Na-Ion · Solid-State · Si-Anode · LTO · LMO · Li-S · LNMO Data vintage: 2024–2026 Focus: 35–50°C operating climate, cost-sensitive market
Read before comparing: Energy density figures are cell-level unless marked (pack). Pack-level is typically 15–30% lower. India ₹/kWh estimates are OEM/pack-level import costs including 15–20% duty — retail replacement is 40–80% higher (₹15,000–22,000/kWh observed for LFP/NMC). Cycle life is to 80% capacity retention at 0.5–1C unless noted. All performance data at standard conditions unless specified.
Full Comparison Table — scroll horizontally
Chemistry Energy Density Cycle Life Cost Safety Hot Weather (35–50°C) Charging Speed Power / Performance India EV Suitability
Status Cell Wh/kg · Pack Wh/kg Cycles to 80% SoH Global $/kWh · India ₹/kWh (est.) Thermal Runaway · Fire Risk Cycle life impact at 45°C Peak C-rate · sensitivity Power density W/kg · notes Rating · best segment
LFP
Lithium Iron Phosphate
● Commercial
90–205 Wh/kg
Pack: 125–160 Wh/kg
CATL next-gen: 205 cell; BYD Blade: ~150. CTP raises pack ratio to ~85% of cell.
2,500–9,000
Typically 3,000–6,000 at 0.5–1C
Premium CTP cells: up to 9,000 cycles
~$81/kWh (BNEF 2025)
₹8,500–12,000/kWh OEM
Stationary: as low as $70/kWh globally. India retail replacement: ₹15,000–18,000/kWh.
 ★ Excellent
Runaway onset: ~270°C. Passes nail penetration without ignition. 60% less heat during failure vs NMC. Low abuse sensitivity.
 ★ Excellent
~20–30% cycle life reduction at sustained 45°C. 94.1% retention after 100 cycles at 45°C (improved electrolytes). Best chemistry for passive/simple cooling in India.
0.5–6C peak
Standard: 1–2C. CATL Qilin/BYD Blade 2.0 Short: up to 6C (8.5 min 10→80%). Low heat sensitivity.
Up to 2,400 W/kg
Good for 2W/3W/passenger EVs. Lower peak power vs NMC. Round-trip efficiency: ~95–97%.
 ★★★★★
Dominant India chemistry. Tata Nexon/Curvv, BYD EVs, MG Comet. Ideal heat/cost profile for India. Primary choice for 2W/3W and cars.
NMC
Nickel Manganese Cobalt (622 / 811)
● Commercial
150–300 Wh/kg
Pack: 140–220 Wh/kg
NMC 622: ~200–240; NMC 811: ~250–300 cell. Pack retains only 60–70% of cell density due to active cooling needs.
1,000–3,000
NMC 622: ~2,000; NMC 811: ~1,000–1,500 at full DoD
Extends significantly with 20–80% SoC window and active thermal management.
~$128/kWh (BNEF 2025)
₹14,000–19,000/kWh OEM
37% premium over LFP. India retail replacement: ₹18,000–22,000/kWh.
 ▲ Moderate
Runaway onset: ~180–210°C. Active cooling mandatory. At 50°C: severe degradation and resistance escalation. NMC 811 is least stable variant.
 ▼ Poor for India
40–50% cycle life reduction at 45°C vs room temp. NMC 811: NCM811 graphite cell loses >60% capacity retention after 450 cycles at 45°C. Requires liquid cooling system adding ~₹1–2 lakh to vehicle cost.
1–3C standard
BMS throttles charging in Indian summers to prevent accelerated degradation. Slower effective charging in 40°C+ weather without pre-conditioning.
1,000–2,000 W/kg
Higher peak power than LFP. Good for highway driving, performance EVs. Efficiency: ~93–95%.
 ★★★☆☆
Used in Hyundai Creta EV, MG ZS, premium imports. Hot-climate degradation and cooling costs make it a poor value vs LFP for most Indian buyers.
LMFP
Lithium Manganese Iron Phosphate
◐ Emerging
160–240 Wh/kg
Pack: 150–190 Wh/kg
ITRI: 210 Wh/kg cell at 2,700 W/kg. Gotion: 240 Wh/kg cell, 190 Wh/kg pack. CATL M3P: ~210 Wh/kg cell. Commercial: 180–210 Wh/kg.
1,800–4,000
Gotion: 1,800–4,000. ITRI: 4,000 at 1C. Slightly below LFP due to higher voltage stress.
~$88–105/kWh (est.)
₹15,000–20,000/kWh OEM
Slight premium over LFP. Cost-competitive per usable kWh due to higher energy density. CATL M3P: 15% cheaper vs NMC per km.
 ★ Excellent
Phosphate-based cathode: runaway ~260–270°C. Passes nail penetration. Mn dissolution resolved in commercial cells. Same safety profile as LFP.
 ★ Very Good
~20–30% cycle life reduction at 45°C. Manganese dissolution (key hot-temp failure mode) has been addressed in commercial CATL M3P/BYD LMFP. Better than NMC; comparable to LFP.
2–3C (CATL M3P)
Higher operating voltage (3.7–3.9V) enables slightly faster charging than LFP. Low heat sensitivity.
~2,700 W/kg (ITRI)
Better power delivery than standard LFP. Good for mid-range passenger EVs.
 ★★★★☆
Strong India candidate. Cost-of-LFP + density-of-NMC. Commercially available 2025–2026 (CATL M3P). Ideal for mid-range cars, e-autos.
NCA
Nickel Cobalt Aluminum
◈ Niche/Premium
200–260 Wh/kg
Pack: 150–210 Wh/kg
Typical composition: 80% Ni, 15% Co, 5% Al. Panasonic 4680 cell (Tesla): targets ~300 Wh/kg. DOE projection: 350 Wh/kg.
800–1,500
At 80% DoD. Extends significantly with shallow cycling (20–80% SoC). Long calendar life if managed well.
$130–170/kWh (est.)
₹18,000–26,000/kWh OEM
Primarily imported into India. High cobalt/nickel dependency. Benchmark Mineral Intelligence: ~$89–95/kWh (2024 global avg.).
 ▼ Poor
Runaway onset: ~150–180°C — worst of common Li-ion. High nickel = high reactivity. Requires sophisticated active cooling. High fire risk without it.
 ▼ Poor for India
Very sensitive above 40°C. High-Ni cathode undergoes accelerated structural degradation (phase transition) in sustained heat. Rapid capacity fade without active thermal management. Essentially requires climate-controlled parking.
1.5–2C standard
BMS heavily throttles in heat. Effective charging speed in Indian summer significantly lower than spec. 800V architecture helps in Tesla/Porsche but not relevant for Indian market.
1,000–2,000 W/kg
High energy enables excellent highway range. Used in performance applications. Efficiency: ~93–95%.
 ★★☆☆☆
Very poor India fit. Thermal fragility in Indian summer + high cost = poor value. Only in fully climate-controlled premium imported EVs. Not recommended.
Na-Ion
Sodium-Ion
◐ Early Commercial
100–175 Wh/kg
Pack: ~130–150 Wh/kg (est.)
CATL Naxtra: 175 Wh/kg cell (highest claimed). Earlier commercial: 120–155 Wh/kg. Pack-level not officially disclosed.
4,000–10,000+
CATL Naxtra: >10,000 (manufacturer claim, not independently verified). General Na-ion: 4,000–8,000.
~$90–110/kWh (early)
₹15,000–19,000/kWh OEM
No lithium, cobalt, or nickel. Projected to undercut LFP at scale. Hard carbon anode cost currently limits savings.
 ★ Excellent
First Na-ion to pass China's GB 38031-2025 traction battery safety standard. Inherently high thermal stability (cathode materials like NaFePO₄ stable to high temps). Very low fire risk.
 ★ Excellent
Stable performance up to 70–80°C (CATL Naxtra: -40°C to +70°C range). Capacity stable at 45°C in early testing. Better hot-climate performance than any lithium-ion except LTO. Ideal for Indian conditions.
5C peak (Naxtra)
CATL Naxtra: 5C peak charge. Excellent fast-charge potential. Low heat sensitivity enables consistent charging in hot weather.
~500–1,500 W/kg
Still developing; lower power density than mature Li-ion. Adequate for city commute EVs and 3-wheelers. Improving with each generation.
 ★★★★★
Outstanding India fit. No lithium dependency (critical for India's import bill), heat-tolerant, safe, ultra-long cycle life. Best for budget city EVs, e-autos, and 2W. Arriving commercially 2025–2026.
Solid-State
Li-Metal + Ceramic/Sulfide Electrolyte
✕ Pre-Commercial
300–500+ Wh/kg
Pack: 250–350 Wh/kg (projected)
Factorial FEST: >390 Wh/kg validated in 100+ Ah cells. Solid Power: ~390 Wh/kg. Semi-solid (WeLion/CATL): 360 Wh/kg in NIO 150 kWh pack. Lab SSB: 800+ Wh/kg.
2,000–5,000 (claimed)
Factorial automotive cell: 600+ cycles validated. Mass-production cycle data unavailable. Long-term durability unverified.
$250–500/kWh (pilot)
Not available in India
3–5× premium over LFP at current pilot scale. Mass production may reduce to ~$150–200/kWh by 2030. India deployment: 2030+ only.
 ★ Excellent
No liquid electrolyte = no flammable component. Eliminates core thermal runaway mechanism. Factorial FEST validated -30°C to +45°C. Fundamentally safer chemistry.
 ★ Good
No liquid electrolyte = no electrolyte decomposition from heat. Ceramic electrolyte thermal expansion/cracking is a manufacturing challenge, not a field-use issue. Better thermal resilience than liquid Li-ion at 45°C.
15→90% in 18 min
Factorial FEST at room temp. High C-rate potential. Manufacturing defects and interface resistance remain challenges at scale.
Targeting 2–3× Li-ion
Theoretical superiority clear. Practical pack-level power data limited. High energy density enables lighter packs for same range.
 ★★☆☆☆
Not India-relevant until 2030+. Premium pricing ($250–500/kWh) makes it irrelevant for India's budget-focused market. First deployments in luxury vehicles globally (Mercedes, BMW, Stellantis demos).
Si-Anode
Silicon-Carbon Anode + NMC/NCA
◐ Early Commercial
260–400 Wh/kg
Pack: 200–280 Wh/kg (est.)
Si-C blend (Sila Titan Silicon): +20% vs graphite NMC, ~260–300 Wh/kg. Si-dominant (Group14 SCC55): up to 50% boost, ~300–400 Wh/kg. First EV: Mercedes EQG (2025–26).
1,500–3,000
Sila Titan Silicon: >2,000 cycles achieved. Group14 SCC55: 1,500–3,000 cycles in 20+ OEM validation programs.
~$130–180/kWh (est.)
₹25,000–40,000/kWh (est.)
Premium over standard NMC. Moses Lake (Sila) and Group14 manufacturing scaling in 2025–26. India: premium import only.
 ▲ Moderate
Based on NMC cathode: similar thermal runaway risk (~180–210°C). Silicon's ~300% volume expansion during cycling can cause SEI cracking if thermally stressed. Requires robust BMS and cooling.
 ▲ Moderate
Silicon expands further with heat, accelerating mechanical degradation. Moderate hot-climate resilience. Similar to NMC in Indian heat but with silicon-specific stress. Needs active cooling at 45°C+.
~2–3C, sub-12 min
Sila/Group14 claim 10–80% in under 12 min. 800V architecture dependency for best charge rates.
~1,500–2,500 W/kg
Excellent energy and power. 20–40% more range per kg vs graphite NMC. Key upgrade path for long-range premium EVs.
 ★★☆☆☆
Not India-relevant currently. Premium pricing, hot-climate silicon stress concerns, and 800V infrastructure dependency make it unsuitable for India's 2025–28 market. Monitor for 2028–30.
LTO
Lithium Titanate Oxide
◈ Commercial / Niche
60–110 Wh/kg
Pack: 50–90 Wh/kg
Lowest energy density of all chemistries here. Toshiba SCiB: ~89 Wh/kg cell. Log9 TiBox (India): 3.2 kWh, ~60–80 Wh/kg. Volumetric: up to 177 Wh/L.
6,000–45,000+
Log9 TiBox: 15,000 cycles. Toshiba SCiB: 20,000+ cycles standard. LTO anode = no lithium plating = no dendrite formation.
$200–500/kWh
₹35,000–60,000+/kWh
High cost per kWh offset by extreme cycle life = competitive TCO for commercial vehicles. Log9 Materials (India) manufactures locally.
 ★ Excellent
Very low fire risk. Wide thermal operating range: -30°C to +60°C. No lithium plating (LTO anode absorbs Li without expansion). Excellent abuse tolerance.
 ★ Best in Class
Exceptional hot-weather performance. LTO cycle life barely affected at 45°C — designed for -30°C to +60°C. 2,000 cycles at 45°C with minimal degradation. WRI India e-bus study: LTO lasted longest in hot Indian conditions.
5–10C standard
Full charge in 5–15 minutes. Ideal for depot flash-charging and opportunity charging. Not sensitive to heat during charging.
3,000+ W/kg
Highest power density here. Excellent for high-current commercial applications. Very high efficiency. Low self-discharge.
 ★★★★☆
Best chemistry for Indian electric buses and commercial EVs. Ultra-long cycle life + fast charging = best TCO in fleet use. Poor for passenger cars (too heavy/bulky). Log9 Materials deploys it in India.
LMO
Lithium Manganese Oxide
— Legacy / Phasing Out
100–150 Wh/kg
Pack: 80–120 Wh/kg
Spinel structure. Was used in older Nissan Leaf (blended LMO+NMC). Still in some hybrids and power tools.
300–700
Rapidly degrades due to Mn²⁺ dissolution into electrolyte (Jahn-Teller effect) and migration to anode. Capacity fade accelerates at high temperature.
$75–90/kWh
₹10,000–14,000/kWh
Cheap raw materials (no Co/Ni). Poor cycle life makes TCO poor. Low cycle life = poor total value despite low upfront cost.
 ▲ Moderate
Spinel structure is more stable than layered oxide. Runaway onset ~250°C. However Mn dissolution at high temp creates gas and accelerates degradation. Moderate abuse tolerance.
 ▼ Very Poor
Manganese dissolution accelerates dramatically above 40°C — the primary failure mode. Worst hot-climate performance of any chemistry. Indian summers destroy LMO batteries significantly faster than rated. Not suitable for India.
1–3C
Decent power delivery (spinel structure allows fast Li-ion diffusion). Not a charging speed concern but cycle life limits total usefulness.
~1,000–2,000 W/kg
Good power-to-weight for its energy density. Used in early hybrids for high-power burst delivery. Declining relevance.
 ★☆☆☆☆
Avoid for India. Hot climate and short cycle life make it commercially nonviable here. Being replaced by LFP and LMFP even in global markets. No significant India EV deployment.
Li-S
Lithium-Sulfur
✕ Pre-Commercial
300–450 Wh/kg
Pack: 200–300 Wh/kg (projected)
Specialist cells achieved 450 Wh/kg (IDTechEx). Theoretical: ~2,600 Wh/kg. Lyten/Zeta Energy in development. First use: aerospace/drones.
200–1,500
Major limitation. Polysulfide shuttle effect dissolves cathode into electrolyte. Best lab results: 2,000+ cycles at very low C-rates. Commercial EV application cycle life: 200–500.
Not commercial
Not available
Sulfur is extremely cheap (~$0.15/kg vs lithium's ~$20/kg). Manufacturing cost of Li-S cells remains high. No established pack cost benchmark.
 ▲ Mixed
Sulfur is non-toxic and abundant. Liquid electrolyte Li-S has flammability risk. Solid-state Li-S would be safer. Thermal runaway behavior at scale unknown. Safety profile unestablished for automotive.
 ▼ Unknown / Poor
Polysulfide shuttle accelerates at higher temperatures — heat worsens the core degradation mechanism. Li-S likely performs worse than LFP in sustained 40°C+ heat. Zero India-relevant data available.
Limited C-rate
Sulfur is a poor conductor. Power density very low. Not suited for fast charging in current form. A fundamental challenge.
~100–500 W/kg
Very low power density — worst here. Sulfur's insulating nature limits current. First viable for weight-sensitive low-power applications (drones, satellites, electric aviation).
 ★☆☆☆☆
No India relevance in foreseeable future. Poor cycle life, hot-climate vulnerability, low power density disqualify it for EVs. Watch for 2030+ aerospace applications only.
LNMO
Lithium Nickel Manganese Oxide
✕ Pre-Commercial
150–220 Wh/kg
Pack: ~140–180 Wh/kg (projected)
Spinel cathode. High voltage: 4.7V vs Li/Li⁺. Theoretical capacity: 146.8 mAh/g = ~650 Wh/kg theoretical. Practical cell: ~220 Wh/kg demonstrated in lab. Toyota targeting 400 km range.
3,000–8,000 (lab)
Lab demonstration: 103 mAh/g retained after 8,000 cycles at 25°C (N-doped LNMO). Commercial data unavailable.
Not commercial
Not available
Raw materials cheap: cobalt-free, low nickel. Production cost unknown. Electrolyte stability at 4.7V remains key unsolved cost driver. Projected: competitive with NMC if solved.
 ★ Good (potential)
Cobalt-free + stable spinel = better than NMC. Runaway onset ~250°C. Manganese dissolution manageable (nickel-stabilized vs pure LMO). Better abuse tolerance than NMC.
 ▲ Moderate
Mn dissolution at elevated temperature is a concern but less severe than LMO due to Ni stabilization. High-voltage operation stresses electrolyte at heat. Better than NMC, worse than LFP for India's conditions.
High rate potential
4.7V operating voltage + 3D spinel = excellent ion diffusion and rate capability. Fast-charge friendly IF electrolyte compatibility is solved.
~1,500–2,500 W/kg
High voltage × decent capacity = good power. Interesting for hybrid/HEV applications where power matters over energy. DOE funding: $2B for Mn-based R&D (2024–27).
 ★★☆☆☆
Not India-relevant before 2030. Cobalt-free profile and manganese abundance in India make it worth watching. Electrolyte instability at 4.7V is the unsolved blocker for commercialization.
Key Takeaways for Indian EV Market
01
LFP is India's present, LMFP is its near future
LFP already dominates India's EV market (Tata Nexon, BYD, MG) for strong reasons: thermal runaway at ~270°C means no fire risk from India's summer heat, cycle life barely affected at 45°C (only ~20–30% reduction), and it's the cheapest commercially available option. LMFP (CATL M3P) offers 15–20% more range at near-identical safety and cost — expect it to replace standard LFP in mid-range India EVs by 2026–27.
02
Sodium-Ion is particularly well-suited to India's specific context
No other emerging chemistry fits India as well: no lithium dependency reduces import risk, exceptional thermal stability means it outperforms LFP in sustained heat, and its low raw material cost can undercut LFP at scale. CATL Naxtra (175 Wh/kg, 5C charge) mass deployment is beginning 2025–26. For India's 2W/3W/budget segments, Na-Ion could be transformative — but the hard carbon anode bottleneck (China holds 95%+ of capacity) must be resolved for India to benefit fully.
03
NMC and NCA carry real, measurable hot-climate risk — and real hidden costs
At 45°C, NMC cycle life drops 40–50% from rated. Above 50°C, NMC shows severe, non-linear degradation. NCA is even worse. Both require liquid active cooling systems (adding ₹1–2 lakh to vehicle cost), precise BMS management, and careful charging habits in summer. India buyers comparing ₹/km lifetime cost should factor this in: an NMC pack that should last 150,000 km might deliver 80,000 km in sustained Indian heat without climate-controlled storage.
04
LTO is the right chemistry for India's electric bus fleet — not for cars
LTO's 60–110 Wh/kg makes it impractical for passenger EVs (too heavy). But its 6,000–45,000 cycle life, 5–10 min fast charging, and near-zero degradation at 45°C make it ideal for depot-charged electric buses. WRI India's e-bus study confirmed LTO outlasted LFP and NMC in hot Indian conditions. Log9 Materials, a Bengaluru startup, already manufactures LTO-based systems locally. The high ₹35,000–60,000/kWh cost is offset by extreme longevity in fleet use.
05
Solid-State, Silicon Anode, Li-S, and LNMO are post-2030 stories for India
All four are technically real and progressing — Factorial's FEST cells are in Mercedes/Stellantis demo vehicles, Sila's silicon anode is in the Mercedes EQG, Li-S has demonstrated 450 Wh/kg. But none of these will be commercially available in India before 2030 in any meaningful volume, and none will be affordable for India's market (₹8–15 lakh EV segments) before 2032–35 at the earliest. India's battery strategy should be built on LFP, LMFP, and Na-Ion today — not on waiting for these technologies.

                                                                                              SOH is deﬁned as the charge capacity of an aged battery cell to
                                                                                          fulﬁll the operating requirements compared with the charge ca-
                                                                                          pacity of a brand-new battery cell (Li et al., 2020b,d). SOH is crucial
                                                                                          to assess the current health condition of the battery. Various
                                                                                          methods have been published in the literature to predict SOH for
                                                                                          lithium-ion batteries. This study divides SOH methods into four
                                                                                          groups: feed-forward algorithms, regression and probabilistic al-
                                                                                          gorithms, and recurrent neural network algorithms, entropy algo-
                                                                                          rithms, and other algorithms.

                                                                                          3.1.2.1. Feed-forward neural network algorithm-based SOH predic-
                                                                                          tion. You et al. (2016) developed a real-time FNN based SOH esti-
                                                                                          mation method for EV batteries. FNN was validated by diverse EV
                                                                                          drive cycles and attained accurate results, with RMSE and MAE of
                                                                                          1.06% and MAE 3.81% respectively under different temperature
                                                                                          settings. Pan et al. (2018) built a novel SOH framework with a
                                                                                          multiple correlation analysis-based ELM network. ELM performed
                                                                                          better than FNN with MAE and RMSE of 1.09% and 1.72%, respec-
                                                                                          tively. Klass et al. (2014) used on-board available battery data to
                                                                                          predict SOH using SVM where SVM achieved RMSE of 0.63% under
                                                                                          changing temperature conditions.

Energy Management (EMM)
General information
In the vehicle, HV energy management regulates the provision of electrical energy and thus
represents the direct connection between the HV energy storage system and the installed
HV electrical components. The energy provided must always be limited to component-
compatible levels. Communication between EMM and the HV components takes place via
bus systems.
The following system functions can be important here:
   -   Operational release and limitation of the current and voltage limits of all HV
       components
   -   Operational activation and deactivation of the HV battery
   -   Current limitation in the HV wiring harness
   -   Coordination of HV battery charging processes
   -   Calculation of electric range
   -   LV wiring system support
   -   Manage departure and loading times
In addition, tasks are derived from functional safety for energy management that require
increased attention during implementation and validation (ASIL requirements/tests).
The EMM is a very comprehensive system that is linked to many other systems. For this
reason, testing requires a very good understanding of the overall system.




Page 1/6

Software Management (SMM)
General information
The software management (SMM) coordinates and monitors the transition between
different operating states (electric driving, hybrid driving, etc.). This means that SMM is
closely linked to drive management (VMM). In addition to the software-side process
monitoring, the SMM takes over the definition of substitute reactions, for example, to be
able to avoid error states of the power electronics by targeted regulation.
The following system functionalities are important here:
   -   Defining target and prohibition states
   -   Higher-level monitoring concepts of the control unit
   -   Plausibility check of driver attendance
   -   Shift-by-Wire Plausibility Check
   -   Interface for diagnostic services and variant coding
   -   Monitoring of sensor data
Software management covers an extremely security-relevant subject area. In addition to an
understanding of the driving system, testing also requires knowledge of data processing.




Page 2/6

Thermal management (TMM)
General information
In hybrid and electric vehicles, thermal management (TMM) regulates the temperatures of
the HV systems and the interior. Since HV components, such as the battery or the electric
motors, only function optimally in a certain temperature range, they must be temperature-
controlled. The TMM monitors the temperatures of these components and climatizes them
in the event of deviations.
The following system functionalities can be important here:
       -   Temperature control of HV systems (battery, electric motors)
       -   Air conditioning of the vehicle interior
       -   Error monitoring of temperature control systems
       -   Optimization of battery performance and range through temperature monitoring
       -   Optimization of charging time through efficient cooling of the battery
       -   Increased service life by minimizing thermal stress
The TMM covers a subject area that is linked to different systems. For this reason, testing
requires a good understanding of the overall system




Page 3/6

Drive management (VMM)
General information
In hybrid and electric vehicles, drive management (VMM) primarily regulates the power
requirements for the corresponding drive components and thus the driving behavior. When
starting up, creeping or during dynamic driving, performance specifications for the electric
powertrain must be coordinated within situational system boundaries through

         SUMMARY
        With the rapid advancement in electric vehicle (EV) technology, efficient battery management has
        become crucial for enhancing performance, safety, and longevity. This research integrates Internet of
        Things (IoT) and artificial intelligence (AI) technology to provide a revolutionary solution to battery
        management in electric vehicles. Our suggested method uses IoT sensors integrated inside the EV battery
        to gather data in real-time while keeping an eye on many factors like voltage, temperature, and current.
        The system can learn from past data and adjust to changing situations thanks to the integration of AI,
        which increases forecast accuracy and battery management efficiency. By continuously analyzing data
        and adjusting parameters in real-time, the system enhances battery performance, extends lifespan, and
        ensures safety by identifying potential issues before they escalate. This data is then processed using a
        neural network-based algorithm to predict battery health, optimize charging protocols, and forecast
        remaining useful life. Battery parameters such as temperature, voltage, and current are collected from the
        sensors, such as temperature sensor, current sensor, and voltage sensor. These values are updated to the
        ESP 32 controller and the IOT (Internet of Things) cloud as thing speak. The battery parameters are stored
        in the Raspberry Pi controller. The support vector machine (SVM) will analyse the battery parameters to
        produce a better output. The SVM produced accuracy, precision, recall and F1-score of 90%, 80%, 78%,
        and 81%, respectively.

        Key words: battery, voltage, current and temperature, SVM, IoT.

Mach1_NITDURGAPUR_Round1/AI & Connected.text:
DELIVERABLE ANALYSIS · AI & CONNECTED MOBILITY ECOSYSTEM

Requirements Framework & Gap Analysis
for the 2035 EV Platform Proposal

Defines what each digital-layer pillar must specify, maps data flows and AI functions, then audits the existing proposal and Suzuki Connect against these requirements.

5 Pillars Analyzed Ola Electric Case · UN R156 · ISO 24089 Status: Gap Analysis
Framing note: The Ola Electric 2021–22 failure is the baseline for every requirement below — 80,000 complaints/month, sensor faults invisible until breakdown, big-bang software pushes with no rollback, and a rider-facing "black box." A credible proposal must either solve each of those failure modes explicitly, or acknowledge the gap. Generic features without data flows and decision logic are insufficient for a proposal at this level.
PART 1

Requirements Framework — What Each Pillar Must Specify

SYSTEM DATA FLOW ARCHITECTURE — 5-LAYER REFERENCE
VEHICLE
Sensors & CAN-bus
BMS · IMU · GPS · Motor current · Fault codes
→
On-board ECU / TCU
Edge pre-processing · OTA slot B
→
Edge Gateway
4G/LTE compression · local anomaly flag
→
Cloud Ingest
Time-series DB · event stream
→
AI / Analytics
CNN/LSTM · Risk scorer · Digital twin
→
Apps & Dashboards
Fleet ops · Driver · Rider
PILLAR 1

Telematics & Vehicle Data

Sub-domain Data Collected (must specify) Flow Path AI Function Decision / Action Enabled
Battery / Power
  • Cell-level voltage & temperature (not pack-average)
  • State-of-Health (SoH) — degradation curve, not binary
  • Charge/discharge C-rate per cycle
  • CNG fuel-pressure & injector status (variant-specific)
 BMS → TCU
TCU → Cloud @ 1Hz
Cloud → Battery ML model 		SoH degradation regression; thermal runaway early-warning classifier; capacity-fade forecast Flag cell imbalance before pack failure; schedule battery swap/service proactively; adjust charging limits per vehicle age
Motion & Powertrain
  • IMU: 3-axis accelerometer + gyroscope at ≥50 Hz
  • Wheel-speed per axle
  • Motor current draw (phase-level)
  • Controller temperature, torque demand vs output
 CAN-bus → ECU
ECU edge-filter → Cloud
Cloud → CNN/LSTM 		Vibration-pattern fault classification (motor bearing wear, inverter fault); road-condition inference from IMU 97%+ motor/inverter fault classification; route-difficulty scoring for duty-cycle calibration
Positioning & Connectivity
  • GPS lock-time and positional accuracy (HDOP)
  • Antenna hardware revision (critical: Ola's GPS mismatch was invisible without this)
  • Connectivity uptime, packet-loss rate per vehicle
 GPS module → TCU
TCU → Cloud metadata 		Hardware-revision mismatch detector; connectivity-stability score feeds OTA risk model Block OTA push to vehicles with unstable connectivity; detect GPS antenna/firmware mismatch before rider impact
Software & Firmware State
  • Firmware version per ECU/module
  • Hardware revision per component
  • Active fault codes (DTC) + historical fault log
  • OTA slot status (A/B), last update timestamp
 ECU → Cloud manifest
Cloud → Risk scorer 		Version/revision matrix compatibility check; fault-history weighting in risk scoring Prevent mismatched firmware reaching riders; auto-rollback to slot A on post-update fault spike
Usage Patterns
  • km/day, trips/day, idle time
  • Charging windows & session duration
  • Duty cycle intensity (urban stop-go vs highway)
 ECU → aggregated daily
Cloud → Digital twin 		Per-vehicle duty-cycle model for fine-tuning failure prediction; charging behavior anomaly detection Customize maintenance intervals per actual usage; detect vehicle misuse or overloading
PILLAR 2

Fleet & Battery Management

Sub-domain What Must Be Specified Flow Path AI Function Decision / Action Enabled
OTA Software Rollout
  • Risk-scoring model features: hardware revision, sensor calibration age, fault history, connectivity stability
  • Cohort size and expansion gate criteria (not just "staged")
  • A/B partition (slot A / slot B) architecture per vehicle
  • Rollback trigger definition (fault-rate threshold post-update)
  • Compliance: UN R156 SUMS + ISO 24089 audit trail
 Cloud → Risk scorer
Risk score → Cohort assign
OTA push → Slot B
Validation pass → Activate 		Risk-score ranking; post-deployment fault-rate monitoring; anomaly triggers rollback signal Zero-downtime update cycle; automatic fleet-wide rollback if fault rate exceeds threshold; audit-ready SUMS log
Fleet Operator Dashboard
  • Multi-vehicle view (500+ vehicles) — not single-vehicle
  • OTA deployment status per vehicle/cohort
  • Active fault summary with severity triage
  • Predicted downtime calendar (when, which vehicles)
  • Battery SoH fleet-wide distribution
 Cloud DB → Fleet API
Fleet API → Operator UI 		Fleet-level anomaly ranking; maintenance workload forecasting; route availability prediction Prioritise workshop slots before predicted failures; pull high-risk vehicles before they strand riders
Battery Lifecycle Management
  • Per-cell SoH trajectory over vehicle lifetime
  • Cycle count vs rated cycle life
  • Thermal event history
  • Second-life eligibility threshold (SoH %)
 BMS → Cloud time-series
Cloud → Degradation model 		Remaining useful life (RUL) regression; second-life readiness classifier Schedule battery replacement at 70–80% SoH before range anxiety impacts riders; flag second-life candidates for stationary storage
PILLAR 3

Driver & Rider Apps

Sub-domain What Must Be Specified Flow Path AI Function Decision / Action Enabled
Driver Interface — Fault UX
  • Plain-language fault triage: exactly three states — "Safe to continue," "Reboot required," "Book service now"
  • No raw DTC codes on primary display
  • Screen-frozen fallback behaviour (audio/haptic)
  • Driver-visible OTA notification before update applies
 ECU fault → Cloud NLP
NLP → Dash message
Message → Driver CTA 		DTC-to-plain-language translation model; severity classification (safe/caution/stop) Driver acts within their competence; eliminates "frozen display — no indicator visible" Ola failure mode
Rider-Facing Data Transparency
  • Explicit disclosure: what data is collected, who sees it, retention period
  • No remote vehicle disable without driver confirmation
  • No silent income-pattern or GPS sale to third parties
  • Driver dashboard showing their own data footprint
 Data policy → In-app
Consent log → Cloud 		None required — policy and UI design decision, not algorithmic Removes #1 e-rickshaw/EV trust barrier; regulatory data-minimisation compliance (DPDP Act 2023)
Proactive Driver Notifications
  • Predicted maintenance alert (vehicle-specific, timed to off-shift)
  • Charging window recommendation (grid load + SoH-aware)
  • OTA update schedule — when and expected duration
 AI prediction → Cloud
Cloud → Driver app push 		Failure prediction output triggers notification; charging optimisation model Driver schedules service voluntarily during downtime, not mid-shift; charging cost optimisation
PILLAR 4

Safety & Predictive Maintenance

Sub-domain What Must Be Specified Flow Path AI Function Decision / Action Enabled
Fault Classification — Motor & Inverter
  • Input signals: vibration (IMU), phase current, temperature
  • Model architecture: CNN/LSTM hybrid (not rule-based threshold)
  • Accuracy benchmark: ≥97% classification (cited in proposal)
  • Fault class taxonomy: bearing wear, winding insulation, IGBT fault, overcurrent
 IMU+current → Edge buffer
Edge → Cloud CNN/LSTM
Output → Fleet alert 		CNN extracts vibration frequency features; LSTM models temporal degradation progression; ensemble reduces false-positive rate Fault type identified before driver notices symptom; maintenance crew dispatched with correct part, not generic inspection
Failure Timeline Prediction
  • Prediction horizon: days-to-failure (not binary fault/no-fault)
  • Baseline accuracy: ±25 days before per-vehicle fine-tuning; ±12 days after (cited)
  • Fine-tuning trigger: per-vehicle usage pattern deviation
  • 100% detection rate for wear-driven failures — quantified from field validation
 Usage history → Cloud model
Per-vehicle fine-tune
Output → Maintenance calendar 		RUL regression with per-vehicle fine-tuning; multi-country heterogeneous fleet validation (India included) Failure flagged ~12 days in advance; service scheduled during off-shift; zero unplanned mid-route breakdown
Digital Twin Validation
  • Twin scope: motor current, thermal behaviour, vibration profile per vehicle model
  • Used as pre-deployment check for every OTA update
  • Triggered by: sensor anomaly flag, hardware revision change, new firmware version
 Sensor telemetry → Twin
OTA package → Twin test
Pass/fail → Rollout gate 		Physics-informed simulation; anomaly deviation detection against expected twin response GPS antenna/firmware mismatch caught in twin before reaching riders; no reactive vehicle-by-vehicle fixes
PILLAR 5

AI / Data Layer Connecting Everything

Component What Must Be Specified Inputs Outputs Connects Which Pillars
Risk-Scoring Engine Feature vector: hardware revision, sensor calibration age, fault history count, connectivity uptime %. Scoring frequency, cohort-size logic, expansion gate thresholds Telemetry + metadata Vehicle risk rank (0–100); cohort assignment; rollout hold flag Telematics → Fleet Management → OTA
CNN/LSTM Fault Classifier Input signal sampling rate; model update cadence; threshold for escalating from "monitor" to "alert" to "ground vehicle" IMU · current · temp Fault class + confidence score; days-to-failure estimate Telematics → Safety → Driver App → Fleet Dashboard
Digital Twin Engine Vehicle model variants covered; deviation tolerance before alert; twin update frequency as real-world data accumulates Sensor stream + OTA package Pass/fail for OTA; deviation anomaly score; validated maintenance schedule Telematics → Safety → Fleet Management → OTA
DTC-to-Language NLP Fault code taxonomy covered; language/dialect support (Hindi, regional); fallback if connectivity lost CAN fault codes Three-state driver instruction; service-booking deep link Telematics → Driver App
Data Governance Layer Retention period per data class; anonymisation before third-party use; driver consent management; DPDP Act 2023 compliance log All telemetry streams Consent-gated data release; audit trail; anonymised research export All pillars → Regulatory & rider trust
PART 2

Gap Analysis — Proposal vs. Suzuki Connect vs. Requirements

ADDRESSED Requirement is substantively covered with specifics
PARTIAL Mentioned but lacks technical depth or data-flow detail
GAP Not addressed — must be added before proposal is credible
Requirement Pillar Proposal Doc Suzuki Connect Gap / What Must Be Added
Cell-level battery telemetry (voltage, temp, SoH per cell) Telematics ADDRESSED GAP Suzuki Connect reports pack-level status only. Proposal correctly specifies cell-level. Needs to add: sampling rate, time-series retention period, and protocol (BMS → CAN → TCU).
CNN/LSTM fault classification (motor, inverter) Safety / AI ADDRESSED GAP Well cited (≥97% accuracy, vibration/current/temp inputs). Missing: fault class taxonomy, false-positive rate target, on-edge vs. cloud inference split, model update cadence.
A/B partition OTA rollback (slot A / slot B) Fleet Mgmt ADDRESSED GAP Proposal correctly cites this as the fix for "scooter won't turn on after update." Needs: rollback trigger definition (which fault-rate threshold activates it) and who authorises manual rollback for fleet ops.
Failure prediction timeline (days-to-failure, field-validated) Safety ADDRESSED GAP Quantified well (±25d → ±12d post fine-tuning; 100% wear-failure detection). Missing: what happens when prediction confidence is low — escalation path and human review workflow.
No remote kill-switch / transparent data use (rider trust) Rider App ADDRESSED GAP Correctly identifies BMS remote-disable as the #1 trust barrier. Needs to reference DPDP Act 2023 compliance specifically, and name what data is not collected (income patterns, route monetisation).
Risk-scored staged OTA rollout Fleet Mgmt ADDRESSED GAP Feature vector listed (HW revision, calibration age, fault history, connectivity). Missing: cohort expansion gate criteria — what metric/threshold unlocks the next cohort? Who approves expansion?
Digital twin pre-deployment validation Safety / AI ADDRESSED GAP Twin scope specified (motor current, thermal, vibration). Needs: which vehicle model variants have twins on day one, twin update latency as real data accumulates, and deviation tolerance threshold.
GPS hardware revision tracking (antenna/firmware mismatch detection) Telematics PARTIAL GAP The Ola GPS mismatch story is cited, but the mechanism to prevent it is not fully specified. Must add: hardware revision logged per component per vehicle in the fleet manifest, with automatic compatibility matrix check on every OTA push. The risk scorer must explicitly include GPS antenna HW revision as a feature.
Driver plain-language fault UX ("safe / reboot / service") Driver App PARTIAL GAP Three states named. Missing: (1) what happens when display itself is frozen — audio/haptic fallback; (2) whether translation happens on-edge (offline capable) or requires connectivity; (3) regional language support (Hindi minimum for Indian fleet).
Fleet operator dashboard (multi-vehicle, not single-owner) Fleet Mgmt PARTIAL GAP Explicitly flagged as absent from Suzuki Connect. Proposal acknowledges fleet-op context but does not describe the dashboard. Must add: key views (OTA deployment status, fault triage, predicted downtime calendar, battery SoH distribution), role-based access (fleet owner vs. mechanic vs. driver), alert routing.
UN R156 SUMS + ISO 24089 compliance Fleet Mgmt / AI PARTIAL GAP Both standards are cited correctly. Not yet specified: what the SUMS audit trail contains (update manifest, vehicle list, rollout timestamp, rollback events), who the nominated SUMS responsible person is, how the ISO 24089 engineering evidence package is generated from the platform.
Continuous telemetry pipeline architecture Telematics / AI PARTIAL GAP Data classes listed correctly. Missing infrastructure detail: streaming protocol (MQTT / AMQP), time-series database choice, data compression at edge (critical for rural connectivity), and what happens when vehicle is offline — local buffer duration and sync behaviour.
CNG variant sensor coverage Telematics PARTIAL GAP Mentioned as "fuel-system sensors for CNG variants" but not elaborated. Needs: which specific CNG sensors (pressure, temperature, injector duty cycle), whether the same CNN/LSTM models apply or CNG requires separate classifiers, and how the AI layer handles dual-fuel variants.
Battery second-life / RUL management Fleet Mgmt GAP GAP Not addressed anywhere in the proposal. For a 2035 vehicle, battery lifecycle economics are a major differentiator. Must add: SoH threshold for replacement vs. second-life routing, RUL regression model, integration with battery recycling/swap partners, and how this data is surfaced to fleet operators.
Data governance / DPDP Act 2023 compliance Rider App / AI GAP GAP Rider data trust is discussed but Indian regulatory compliance is not named. Must add: data retention periods per class, consent collection mechanism, right-to-erasure workflow, and what is excluded from third-party data sharing. Critical for commercial fleet operators operating under DPDP Act 2023.
Offline / degraded-connectivity fail-safes Telematics / Safety GAP GAP Indian rural and peri-urban routes have intermittent 4G. The proposal assumes connectivity for AI inference but doesn't specify: local edge inference capability for fault detection when offline, data buffer size/duration, prioritisation of what syncs first when connectivity restores.
Charging infrastructure integration Fleet Mgmt / Driver App GAP GAP No mention of integration with public/fleet charging networks. For EV fleet deployment, the platform should surface: nearest compatible charger, real-time charger availability, smart charging scheduling (off-peak grid load), and charging session data back into the BMS telemetry loop.
Maintenance workflow integration (workshop, parts, scheduling) Fleet Mgmt / Safety GAP GAP Predictive maintenance outputs a "fault in 12 days" signal — but what happens next is unspecified. Must add: how the fleet dashboard connects to workshop scheduling, spare-parts inventory pre-positioning, and technician mobile interface showing which fault class to expect before the vehicle arrives.
Model drift monitoring & retraining pipeline AI Layer GAP GAP Proposal cites accuracy benchmarks at training time, but doesn't address what happens as the fleet ages and data distribution shifts. Must add: model performance monitoring in production, drift detection trigger, retraining cadence, and whether fine-tuned per-vehicle models are retrained continuously or in batches.
PART 3

Priority Additions for Proposal Readiness

Items are grouped by urgency. Red = proposal is not credible without it. Amber = gaps a sophisticated evaluator will probe. Blue = differentiators that strengthen the proposal.

CRITICAL · FLEET MGMT

Define Fleet Operator Dashboard Screens

The proposal has no fleet-ops UI specification. Add: OTA cohort status view, fault severity heat-map across 500+ vehicles, predicted downtime calendar, and SoH distribution chart. Without this, the platform is indistinguishable from Suzuki Connect's single-owner model.

CRITICAL · REGULATORY

SUMS Audit Trail & DPDP Act 2023 Compliance

Cite UN R156 and ISO 24089 but then show what the audit log contains: update manifest, vehicle ID, rollout timestamp, rollback events, and sign-off chain. Add a data governance matrix specifying retention, consent, and third-party exclusions under India's DPDP Act 2023.

CRITICAL · TELEMATICS

GPS Hardware Revision — Explicit Mismatch Prevention

The Ola GPS story is the opening case study, but the solution mechanism is underspecified. Add: hardware revision logged per component in the fleet manifest; OTA compatibility matrix check blocks push if antenna HW revision is incompatible with new firmware. Name this as a specific risk-scorer feature.

CRITICAL · SAFETY

Offline Edge Inference Capability

Indian fleet routes include rural and low-connectivity corridors. Specify: which fault classifiers run on-edge without cloud connectivity, local data buffer duration (minimum 72h recommended), and sync priority queue when connectivity restores. A cloud-only AI layer is a single point of failure for this market.

IMPORTANT · FLEET MGMT

OTA Cohort Gate Criteria (not just "staged")

The proposal says cohorts are staged but never defines the expansion gate. Add: the specific metric (fault-rate per 1,000 km, rollback events per cohort), the threshold that unlocks the next cohort, the waiting period, and who approves expansion — automated or human sign-off.

IMPORTANT · DRIVER APP

Driver UX Offline Fallback & Language Support

Plain-language fault messages must work when connectivity is lost. Specify: local DTC-to-language lookup table on-device, audio/haptic alert if display is frozen (closing Ola's frozen-screen failure mode), and minimum regional language support (Hindi + Bengali/Tamil/Telugu for initial fleet regions).

IMPORTANT · FLEET MGMT

Maintenance Workflow Integration

A "12-day fault prediction" is only valuable if it triggers a workshop booking. Add: fleet dashboard → workshop scheduling integration, spare-parts pre-positioning signal from fault class output, and technician mobile view showing expected fault type before vehicle arrives.

IMPORTANT · FLEET MGMT

Battery Second-Life & RUL Management

A 2035 vehicle proposal with no battery lifecycle economics is incomplete. Add SoH replacement threshold (commonly 70–80%), RUL regression output to fleet dashboard, and how expired batteries are flagged for second-life (stationary storage) vs. recycling. This is a cost and sustainability differentiator.

DIFFERENTIATOR · AI LAYER

Model Drift Monitoring & Retraining Pipeline

Benchmarks cited (97% accuracy, ±12d prediction) are training-time metrics. Add: production performance monitoring cadence, drift detection trigger (e.g., false-positive rate rising >5%), retraining pipeline (batch vs. continuous), and whether per-vehicle fine-tuned models update automatically or require fleet-ops approval.

DIFFERENTIATOR · FLEET MGMT

Charging Infrastructure Integration

Bind the AI layer to the charging network: nearest compatible charger, real-time availability, smart charging schedule (off-peak + SoH-aware charge rate), and charging session data looped back into the BMS telemetry. This closes the energy management loop and is a strong fleet-operator selling point.

DIFFERENTIATOR · TELEMATICS

CNG Variant Sensor Specification

Clarify which CNG sensors are in scope (pressure, temp, injector duty cycle), whether CNN/LSTM models are shared with EV variants or require separate training data, and how dual-fuel variant telemetry is handled. A single vague line on "fuel-system sensors" is insufficient for a proposal covering India's mixed fleet reality.

DIFFERENTIATOR · AI LAYER

Telemetry Pipeline Infrastructure

Name the streaming protocol (MQTT preferred for low-bandwidth IoT), time-series database, edge compression ratio target, and what happens during extended offline periods. This transforms the data layer from a concept into a buildable architecture that procurement and engineering teams can evaluate.

SOURCES: Ola Electric 2021–22 field data · UN Regulation No. 156 (SUMS) · ISO 24089 · India DPDP Act 2023 · Field validation pipeline — 3-country heterogeneous fleet (2026) · Suzuki Connect product specification (Arena/NEXA TCU layer) · CNN/LSTM motor fault classification industry benchmarks

        AI-Enhanced Battery Management Systems for Electric
        Vehicles: Advancing Safety, Performance, and Longevity
        Md. Khaja Farman1, Jarabana Nikhila1, A. Bhavya Sreeja1, B. Sai Roopa1, K. Sahithi1, Devineni Gireesh Kumar2*

        1
         U G Students, Department of EEE, B V Raju Institute of Technology, Narsapur, 502313, Telangana, India
        2
         Associate Professor, Department of EEE, B V Raju Institute of Technology, Narsapur, 502313, Telangana, India


                      Abstract. Electric vehicles (EVs) are essential to lowering carbon emissions and solving global
                      environmental issues. The battery powers EVs, making its management crucial to safety and performance.
                      As a self-check system, a Battery Management System (BMS) ensures operating dependability and
                      eliminates catastrophic failures. As batteries age, internal resistance increases and capacity decreases, hence
                      a BMS monitors battery health and performance in real time. EV energy storage systems (ESSs) need a
                      complex BMS algorithm to maintain efficiency. Using battery efficiency calculations that account for
                      charging time, current, and capacity, this approach should reliably forecast the battery's SoC and SoH. As
                      batteries age, internal resistance increases, reducing constant current (CC) charging time. By analyzing these
                      changes, the SoH can be predicted more precisely. Conventional methods for estimating SoC and enhancing
                      BMS performance, such as deep neural networks, are used to minimize error rates. However, as the battery
                      ages, AI approaches have gained prominence for their ability to provide precise diagnostics, fault analysis,
                      and thermal management. These AI-driven techniques significantly enhance safety and reliability during
                      charging and discharging cycles. To further ensure safety, a fault diagnosis algorithm is integrated into the
                      BMS. This algorithm proactively addresses potential issues, thus maintaining the efficiency and safety of
                      the battery. The effectiveness of the proposed BMS algorithms are demonstrated through its successful
                      application in an ESS, validating its capability to manage the battery’s state, enhance performance, and
                      ensure operational sustainability in EVs.

Design the Ideal Ride-Service Vehicle for India 2035. Determine the optimal vehicle size,
seating configuration, body style, powertrain strategy and digital ecosystem for intra-city,
inter-city, shared and premium mobility services. The solution should maximize customer
satisfaction, driver earnings, fleet profitability and scalability across India.

        2. Vehicle Concept
Body Style — Compact Sedan

A sedan is the right call for ride-share. The separate boot keeps passenger and luggage space distinct,
and the silhouette reads as professional — something riders respond to. No compromise here.

Size — Subcompact B-Segment

3,995 mm long, ~2,450 mm wheelbase. Identical footprint to both the Aeris and Dzire Tour S. Big
enough to seat adults comfortably, small enough to navigate Indian city traffic and park without
drama.

Seating — 5-Seat, 2-Row (Fleet-Configured)

Standard 2+3 layout, but rear-biased — the paying passengers sit there. Flat floor (EV advantage: no
transmission tunnel), rear AC vents, and durable leatherette upholstery built for high-turnover use.
Boot target: 400+ litres, matching the Aeris over the Dzire Tour S.

Target Segments

Primary — Ride-share fleet operators (Ola, Uber, BluSmart): The Dzire Tour S proved the
formula. This takes the same commercial-ready brief and electrifies it for operators already running
EV fleets in metro cities.

Secondary — City cab aggregators: Clean vehicle mandates in metros are pushing aggregators
toward EV. A purpose-built commercial EV sedan fills a gap — the Tiago EV is too small, and nothing
above it is fleet-priced.




        3. Powertrain and Energy Strategy

To Build a EV sedan for Indian Fleet use , consider current market problems. ​

    1.​ Powertrain System: In general EV market, Car manufacturers use a simple PMSM
        system, coupled with single-speed automatic transmission.
         #Don’t go with 45bhp, but prefer an 80-100bhp motor.

PMSM (Permanent Magnet Synchronous Motor):

       Lifespan — Motor windings and rotor last 15–20+ years / 200,000+ km; bearings are
       the main wear item; inverter typically 10–15 years.

       Cost (India) — Motor alone: ₹50,000–1,50,000 for passenger EV; full powertrain unit
       (motor + SiC inverter + single-speed gearbox): ₹1.5–4 lakh depending on power
       class.

       Safety — Inherently safe; main risks are inverter shoot-through (managed by gate
       drivers) and demagnetization above ~150°C, both handled by BMS/controller logic.

       Hot weather (35–50°C) — Copper winding resistance rises ~0.4%/°C so efficiency
       drops 1–2% at 45°C; more critically, NdFeB magnet remanence (Br) drops ~0.1%/°C
       causing flux weakening and slight torque reduction — water-cooled motors handle
       this well, air-cooled budget designs struggle.

       Regen efficiency — Recovers 60–80% of braking energy; effective mainly above
       ~15 km/h, negligible at very low speeds.

       Peak efficiency — 93–97% at the optimal operating point; drops meaningfully at low
       speeds and light loads (iron losses dominate there), which is why Indian city
       stop-start driving isn't as efficient as highway.

7. Roadmap to scale:

The spares and accessories segment was ₹5,571 crore in FY16, ~10% of total revenue,
growing at 19% YoY — faster than car sales themselves. Two-thirds of that is spares. This
isn't a side business, it's a core recurring revenue engine built entirely on ICE vehicles.

Here's the real paragraph:



The Infrastructure Transition Risk

Maruti's spares and service network — 3,614 outlets, 480+ genuine parts distributors,
growing at 19% YoY — is currently one of its most reliable revenue streams, generating
roughly 10% of total company revenue and outpacing car sales growth. But this entire
ecosystem is built for ICE. EV servicing is fundamentally different: fewer mechanical parts,
high-voltage systems, battery diagnostics, OTA software. As Maruti transitions its fleet to EV,
this recurring revenue model needs to be rebuilt in parallel — EV-certified technicians,
battery health infrastructure, updated parts network. The transition window matters: whoever
builds EV service density first owns the operator trust. For this car to sustain the same
post-sale revenue logic, the service infrastructure needs to be EV-ready at launch, not
retrofitted later.
